rules.text: Keep the package in three layers: `stock/models/`, `stock/storage/`, `stock/commands/`. Each layer may call only the layer below it.
Commands never touch storage files directly; they go through the storage interface.
Models know nothing about storage. A model module must not reach into `stock/storage/`.
Put domain rules on the model that owns the data, not in the command that happens to need them.
Prefer the simplest design that solves the actual problem; reuse an existing pattern before you add a new layer.
Do not add a new abstraction for a single caller. Wait for the second real use before you extract it.
Keep `stock/commands/` thin: parse the request, call the domain, render the reply. Nothing else lives there.
When a command module grows past a few hundred lines, move the domain work into `stock/models/` and keep only orchestration.
Do not create cyclic dependencies between modules. If two models need each other, the shared part belongs in a third module.
A model module may depend on another model module only when the domain says one owns the other.
Treat the storage interface as a contract. Every backend must honour the same read, write and delete semantics.
Add a capability to the storage interface only when every backend can support it.
Keep backend-specific shortcuts inside the backend. Callers must never branch on which backend is active.
Stock levels are derived from the movements ledger; never write a quantity that the ledger cannot explain.
The ledger is append-only. Correct a bad movement with a reversing movement, never by editing or deleting it.
Every movement records an item, a location, a signed quantity and a reason code.
Use a fixed set of reason codes for movements, e.g. `receive`, `ship`, `transfer`, `count`, `scrap`. Add new codes in one place.
A transfer between two locations is one movement with two legs; write both legs together or neither.
On-hand quantity must never go below zero unless the location explicitly allows backorders.
Reserved quantity can never exceed on-hand quantity at the same location.
Available quantity is on-hand minus reserved. Compute it; do not persist it.
Do not cache derived quantities in the model. Recompute from the source data or invalidate on every write.
Keep quantities as integers in the smallest unit the item is counted in. Never use floats for stock counts.
Each item has exactly one base unit of measure. Pack sizes convert to the base unit at the edge.
Unit conversions live in `stock/models/units.py`. Do not inline a conversion factor in a command.
Reject a conversion between units of different dimensions, such as `kg` to `each`, at the model level.
Round only at the display edge. Domain math works on exact integer base units.
An SKU is an opaque identifier. Do not parse meaning out of its parts in domain code.
SKUs are case-insensitive for lookup but keep their original case for display.
Normalise SKU input once, at the boundary where it enters the domain, and pass the normal form everywhere else.
Never reuse a retired SKU for a new item. Retired SKUs stay reserved forever.
Archive items instead of deleting them, because the ledger still points at them.
A location is identified by warehouse and bin, e.g. `MAIN/A-03-2`. Treat the pair as one value.
Bins belong to exactly one warehouse. Moving a bin to another warehouse is a new bin.
Keep the location hierarchy shallow: warehouse, then bin. Do not add zones or aisles without a concrete use case.
A supplier record holds identity and contact data only. Prices and lead times live on the item-supplier link.
An item can have many suppliers, but at most one preferred supplier at a time.
Reorder points are per item and location, not per item. A global reorder point hides local shortages.
A reorder suggestion is a read-only report. It must never create a purchase or a movement by itself.
Cycle counts produce adjustment movements; they never overwrite the on-hand figure directly.
An adjustment records the counted quantity and the expected quantity, so the variance can be audited later.
Reservations reference an order or a caller-supplied key. Releasing a reservation twice must be a no-op.
Make every write operation idempotent when the caller supplies a request key. Replaying the same key returns the first result.
Read first, then write. Never assume the stored state matches what the command saw at the start.
Every write must converge: running it twice with the same input leaves the same stored state.
Group related writes in one storage transaction. A partial write must leave no trace.
Validate the whole request before the first write. Do not interleave checks and writes.
Domain invariants are checked in the model, not in each command. Commands trust the model to enforce them.
When you add a new invariant, add a check that scans existing stored data for violations first.
Do not widen what the model accepts just to make one command easier. Change the command instead.
Model identity is the SKU for items, the code for locations, and the code for suppliers. Do not add surrogate ids without a reason.
Equality between two models compares identity fields only, not every attribute.
Keep model attributes plain: strings, integers, decimals, lists and nested models. No live handles or file objects.
Money values use `decimal.Decimal` with an explicit currency code. Never mix currencies in one sum.
Unit cost belongs to the movement that brought the stock in, not to the item.
Valuation reports read cost from receipt movements. Do not add a running cost field to items.
Do not denormalise supplier names into movements. Keep the supplier code and look the name up.
Prefer one clear source of truth for each fact. If a fact is stored twice, one copy must be marked as derived.
Model methods return new values or mutate their own instance. They never write to storage.
The storage layer returns model instances, never raw rows or dicts, to code outside `stock/storage/`.
Keep row-to-model mapping in one module per backend. Do not scatter field mapping across commands.
Field names in stored data match the model attribute names. Renaming one means a migration for the other.
Do not remove or rename a stored field in place. Add the new field, migrate, then drop the old one in a later release.
Each data file carries a schema version. Readers refuse to touch a file with a newer version than they know.
Migrations live in `stock/storage/migrations/` as numbered modules, e.g. `0007_add_bin_capacity.py`.
A migration runs forward only. Write a new migration to undo a bad one; never edit one that has shipped.
Every migration must be safe to run twice. Check whether the change is already present before applying it.
A migration touches data only. Do not change domain behaviour in the same commit as a migration.
Before a migration rewrites a data file, keep a copy next to it with a `.bak` suffix until the run completes.
Migrations must not call domain code that may change later. Copy the small piece of mapping they need.
Each migration ships with a fixture of the old layout and a check that the new layout loads.
Never migrate data silently on read. Upgrades run only through the explicit `stock migrate` command.
Writes go to a temporary file first, then replace the target in one rename, so a crash never leaves half a file.
Hold the data-directory lock for the whole read-modify-write cycle, not only for the write.
Take locks in a fixed order: data directory first, then item files. Never take them in reverse.
Release every lock on every path out of a write, including early returns.
Do not hold a storage lock while waiting on user input.
A read-only command must never take a write lock.
Backends must preserve the order in which movements were appended. Readers rely on that order.
Assign each movement a monotonically increasing sequence number at write time. Do not reuse gaps.
Sequence numbers are per data directory, not per item, so a full replay is a single ordered scan.
Snapshots of on-hand levels are a cache over the ledger. Rebuilding them from the ledger must give the same numbers.
If a snapshot and the ledger disagree, the ledger wins. Rebuild the snapshot; never patch the ledger.
Keep snapshot rebuild cheap enough to run on every `stock verify`.
`stock verify` checks every invariant against stored data and changes nothing.
When you add a new invariant to the model, add the matching check to `stock verify` in the same change.
The in-memory backend exists for fast checks. It must follow the same invariants as the file backends.
Do not add backend features that only the in-memory backend can do. Every backend is a first-class citizen.
New backends start under `stock/storage/contrib/` and move to the core package only after a release of real use.
Keep the storage interface small: get, list, put, append movement, and transaction. Resist adding query methods.
Filtering and sorting happen in the domain layer over plain iterables, unless a backend proves too slow.
A backend may add an index for speed, but the result of every interface call must not change because of it.
Listing methods return items in a stable order (SKU ascending) so reports diff cleanly between runs.
Pagination on list calls uses an opaque cursor, not an offset, so concurrent writes do not shift pages.
Never expose a backend cursor or row id outside `stock/storage/`.
Data directories are self-contained. Two data directories must never share a file.
Do not depend on file modification times to detect changes. Use the stored sequence number.
Keep stored files human-readable where the backend allows, so an operator can inspect them with `less`.
A stored record must be readable without running any `stock` code: no pickles, no custom binary blobs.
Do not use `pickle` or `marshal` for persisted data. Persisted formats must be stable across Python versions.
CSV exports use a fixed column order documented in `docs/formats.md`. Adding a column means adding it at the end.
Treat the CSV column order as a public contract. Downstream sheets depend on it.
Never reorder or rename export columns in a patch release.
Bulk loads go through the same model checks as single writes. There is no fast path that skips invariants.
Bulk loads are all-or-nothing per file. If one row is invalid, nothing from that file is written.
A bulk load reports how many rows it accepted and how many it skipped, in one summary at the end.
Keep a reference to the source row on each loaded record until the load commits, so a rejected batch can be traced.
Model fields that are lists keep insertion order and reject duplicates.
Use `None` only for "unknown". Use zero or an empty value for "known to be nothing".
Do not overload one field with two meanings. Add a second field instead.
Enumerated values such as reason codes use `enum.Enum` members, not bare strings, inside the domain.
Convert enum members to their string values only at the storage and display edges.
Adding an enum member is a compatible change. Removing or renaming one needs a migration.
Item attributes that vary by warehouse, like reorder points or bin defaults, live on a per-location record, not on the item.
Keep the item record small: SKU, name, base unit, status, and tags. Everything else is linked by SKU.
Tags are free-form lower-case labels for grouping. Do not attach domain meaning to a specific tag.
Status changes on an item go through one method that checks allowed transitions, e.g. `active -> archived`.
Archived items cannot receive new stock. They can still ship what is already on hand.
Model the item lifecycle as a small state machine. Draw it in `docs/architecture.md` when you change it.
A reservation has its own lifecycle: `held`, `released`, `consumed`. Do not infer state from other fields.
Consuming a reservation and writing the shipment movement happen in one transaction.
Expired reservations are released by `stock sweep`, never as a side effect of an unrelated read.
Reads never mutate stored state. A read that cleans up as it goes is a hidden write.
Keep the domain deterministic: the same inputs and stored state always give the same result.
Pass the active warehouse into domain code as an argument instead of reading it from a module-level global.
Pass randomness in as an argument as well. Domain code must not call `random` directly.
Domain code is pure Python. It must not read files, the network or the process state.
Side effects live at the edges: storage below, the terminal above. The middle is plain functions over models.
Keep reports separate from commands that write. A report module may read but never append a movement.
Each report lives in `stock/reports/` and takes models in, returns rows out. Rendering is done by the caller.
Reports must not call each other. Share the calculation through a function in `stock/models/` instead.
When two reports disagree on a number, the bug is in the shared calculation. Fix it there, not in one report.
Aggregations over the ledger must be associative so they can be computed per chunk and merged.
Do not let a report silently skip unknown SKUs. Count them and show the count.
Keep the per-location stock view and the per-item stock view backed by the same function.
A bin that holds stock cannot be removed. Move or scrap its contents first.
Model negative stock as a visible state with its own report, not as a hidden clamp to zero.
Do not round quantities when you split a pack into units. If it does not divide evenly, reject the split.
Lot and serial tracking is opt-in per item. Items without it must not carry empty lot fields.
A serial number belongs to exactly one item and is unique across the whole data directory.
Lots are identified by item plus lot code. The same lot code on two items is two different lots.
Pick from lots in the order they were received by default; any other order must be an explicit choice by the caller.
Keep the picking strategy a plain function that takes candidate lots and returns an ordered list.
Strategies are swapped by passing a different function, not by subclassing the picker.
Prefer composition over inheritance for models. A deep class tree in `stock/models/` is a review blocker.
Do not use metaclasses or class decorators that rewrite models at runtime.
Avoid mixins in the domain layer. Shared behaviour goes into a plain function both models call.
Keep the public surface of `stock` small. Anything not documented in `docs/api.md` is internal and may change.
Internal modules start with an underscore, e.g. `stock/storage/_lock.py`. Nothing outside the package may reach into them.
When you move a public model to a new module, keep the old path working for one minor release.
Do not change the meaning of an existing public model method. Add a new method with a new name instead.
Treat the stored data layout as a public contract, even more than the Python API. Users keep data for years.
A change to stored data layout needs a design note in `docs/decisions/` before code review.
Design notes are numbered and never deleted. Supersede an old note with a new one that links back.
Name domain concepts after the words warehouse staff use: on hand, reserved, available, receipt, shipment.
Use the same term for a concept in code, stored data and user-facing text. Do not call it `qty` in one place and `amount` in another.
Keep a glossary of domain terms in `docs/glossary.md` and update it when you add a concept.
Do not invent a synonym for an existing domain term in a new module.
Prefer `receipt` for stock coming in and `shipment` for stock going out. Avoid `in`/`out` as nouns.
When a feature needs a new domain concept, write down its invariants before you write its model.
Each new model gets a short section in `docs/architecture.md` listing what it owns and who may change it.
Do not grow a model into a god object. If a model has more than one reason to change, split it.
Keep the dependency graph between packages pointing one way: commands -> reports -> models <- storage.
Storage depends on models to build instances; models never depend on storage. Keep that arrow one-way.
Do not pass the storage object into a model method. Load what the model needs and hand it the values.
A command that needs two backends at once, such as a copy between data directories, opens each through the same interface.
Copying data between backends replays the ledger in order. Never copy derived snapshots across.
Keep backend selection in one factory function at the top of the command layer.
A data directory records which backend wrote it. Opening it with a different backend is refused.
Make storage reads streaming where the backend allows. Do not load the whole ledger into memory for one item.
For large data directories, keep a per-item offset index so single-item reads stay fast.
Indexes are rebuildable from the primary data. Deleting an index file must never lose information.
Do not store the same movement in two files for speed. Use an index that points at the one copy.
Concurrent writers from two processes are supported only through the lock. Do not add a second coordination path.
Treat a stale lock as a real lock until its owner process is confirmed gone.
Lock files record the owning process id and host, so `stock doctor` can explain who holds them.
Never break a lock automatically in a write command. Breaking a lock is a separate, explicit operation.
Nested transactions are not supported. Opening one inside another is a programming fault and must be caught in review.
A transaction holds model instances, not storage rows. Commit converts them in one pass.
Do not perform slow work, like report rendering, inside an open transaction.
Keep transactions short. Gather input, then open the transaction, write, and close it.
A rollback must leave the data directory byte-for-byte as it was before the transaction.
When a write affects many items, sort them by SKU before writing so concurrent runs touch files in the same order.
Item merges, where two SKUs turn out to be the same product, write a merge movement pair; they never rewrite history.
After a merge, the retired SKU resolves to the surviving one on lookup, and the mapping is kept forever.
Splits of one SKU into two follow the same rule: new movements, old history untouched.
Supplier codes are stable. Renaming a supplier changes its display name, not its code.
Lead time is stored in whole days on the item-supplier link. Do not mix units for durations.
Minimum order quantity and pack multiple live on the item-supplier link, not on the item.
Reorder quantity suggestions respect the supplier's pack multiple and minimum order quantity.
Keep the reorder calculation a pure function of on-hand, reserved, incoming, reorder point and pack rules.
Incoming stock from open purchases counts toward availability only in reorder math, never in on-hand.
Keep purchases out of the core model until a real user asks. `stock` tracks movements, not procurement.
Before adding a feature, check whether it is inventory tracking or a different product. Decline scope creep politely.
A model change that alters what is stored needs a matching update to the sample data in `examples/`.
Keep `examples/` data small and realistic: a few warehouses, a few dozen items, a few hundred movements.
Sample data uses obviously fake supplier names and codes, e.g. `ACME-001`.
Never ship real customer inventory data in fixtures, examples or issue attachments.
Keep identifiers in stored data stable across versions; a reformat of SKUs or bin codes is a migration.
Prefer explicit fields over positional tuples in stored records, so a reader can tell what each value is.
When a model needs a computed property, make it cheap. Expensive values belong in a report, not a property.
Avoid hidden I/O in properties. Reading a model attribute must never trigger a storage call.
Do not lazy-load related records through attribute access. Load them explicitly in the command.
Write the commit subject in the imperative mood: `Add reorder report`, not `Added reorder report`.
Keep the commit subject under 72 columns so it reads well in one-line history views and on GitHub.
Use the commit body to say why the change exists; the diff already shows what changed.
Separate the subject from the body with one blank line.
Start each commit subject with a conventional type such as `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, or `chore:`.
Add a scope in parentheses when the change sits in one area: `fix(ledger): keep reservation counts in sync`.
Do not end the commit subject with a period.
Make each commit do one thing; split an unrelated cleanup into its own commit.
Every commit on `main` must pass the full check suite on its own, so `git bisect` stays usable.
Never land commits titled `wip`, `fixup`, or `tmp` on `main`; squash or reword them first.
Reference the issue in the commit body with `Refs #123` or `Fixes #123`, not in the subject.
Do not mix regenerated files with hand edits in one commit unless the edit caused the regeneration.
Credit pair work with a `Co-authored-by:` trailer at the end of the body.
Sign off every commit with `git commit -s`; the DCO check blocks unsigned commits.
Sign release and tag commits with a verified GPG or SSH key.
Never commit tokens, passwords, or private keys, even in a commit that a later commit removes.
Mark a breaking public change with a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer that names the old and the new behaviour.
Keep the default `Revert "..."` subject that `git revert` writes, and add the reason in the body.
Prefer several small commits that tell a story over one large commit that mixes steps.
Commit a file move or rename on its own so Git tracks the history across the rename.
Put pure formatting changes in a separate commit and list its hash in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`.
Do not merge `main` into your feature branch; rebase onto it instead.
Amend or reword only commits that you have not pushed to a shared branch.
Write commit messages in English, even when the linked issue is in another language.
Say in the body when a commit changes the on-disk inventory layout, so reviewers know to check upgrades.
Do not put emoji in commit subjects; they break the release-note script that parses the type prefix.
Write the body in present tense, describing the state after the commit.
Wrap the commit body at 72 columns.
Link the design discussion or ADR in the body when the commit carries out a decision made there.
Never commit files from your home folder, editor workspace files, or macOS Finder metadata.
Stage files by name or with `git add -p`; avoid `git add .` in a dirty tree.
Put personal ignore patterns in `.git/info/exclude`, not in the shared `.gitignore`.
Commit a lockfile refresh by itself with the subject `chore(deps): refresh lockfile`.
Do not commit binary fixtures over 1 MB; generate them in the test run or keep them out of the repo.
Use invented SKUs and supplier names in committed sample data, never a real customer's inventory.
Create feature branches from an up-to-date `main`: `git switch -c feat/reorder-report origin/main`.
Name branches `<type>/<short-topic>`, for example `fix/negative-on-hand` or `docs/warehouse-guide`.
Add the issue number to the branch name when one exists: `fix/412-duplicate-sku`.
Use lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens in branch names; no spaces or slashes beyond the type prefix.
Keep branches short-lived; merge or close a branch within a week of its first push.
Delete the remote branch after the PR merges; GitHub does this when you enable auto-delete.
Never push directly to `main`; every change goes through a pull request.
Treat `release/*` branches as protected; only maintainers push to them, and only through backport PRs.
Rebase onto the latest `main` before you request review so reviewers see a current diff.
Do not force-push a branch that another person has commits on without asking them first.
Open one PR per branch; do not reuse a merged branch for new work.
Close your own stale branches each month; a branch untouched for 30 days is a candidate for deletion.
Prefix experimental branches with your handle, as in `tony/spike-sqlite-wal`, so others know not to build on them.
Clean up the commit series with `git rebase -i origin/main` before you mark a PR ready.
After review starts, push follow-up commits instead of rewriting history, so reviewers can see what changed.
After you resolve rebase conflicts, run the full check suite again before you push.
Never rebase `main` or any release branch; those histories are fixed.
Keep the original author on commits you rebase or cherry-pick from another person.
Keep pull requests small: aim for under 400 changed lines, not counting generated files and fixtures.
Give each PR one purpose; a feature, a refactor, and a dependency bump are three PRs.
Land a preparatory refactor in its own PR before the feature that needs it.
Write the PR title like a commit subject, with the conventional type: `feat(report): add aging buckets`.
Treat the PR title as the final squash commit subject; edit it when the scope changes during review.
Fill in the PR description with what changed, why, and how you verified it.
Use the template in `.github/pull_request_template.md`; do not delete its sections, write `n/a` instead.
Give reviewers exact steps to reproduce the old behaviour and to check the new one.
Add a short Risk section to the PR description when the change touches stored inventory data.
Do not paste a generated wall of text into the PR description; keep it to what a reviewer needs.
List known follow-up work in the description and link the issues you opened for it.
Link the issue the PR closes with `Closes #123` so GitHub closes it on merge.
A typo or a one-line fix does not need an issue first; anything larger does.
Open an issue or a discussion before a PR that adds a new command or changes the storage format.
Open a draft PR early to share direction; mark it ready only when checks pass and the description is complete.
Do not request reviewers on a draft PR unless you ask them a specific question in a comment.
Before you mark a PR ready, tick every item in the template checklist that applies and strike out the rest.
Wait for CI to pass before you request review; reviewers skip red PRs.
Review your own diff on GitHub before you ask anyone else to; you will catch half the comments yourself.
Leave your own review comments on tricky hunks to explain them before reviewers ask.
Revert unrelated whitespace, renames, and drive-by edits before you request review.
If you find an unrelated bug while you work, open an issue or a separate PR for it.
Mark generated files as generated in `.gitattributes` so GitHub collapses them in the diff.
Add one type label and one area label to every PR, such as `type/bug` and `area/ledger`.
Set the milestone to the release you target; maintainers move it if the PR slips.
Assign the PR to yourself; the assignee is the person who drives it to merge.
Let CODEOWNERS pick the first reviewer; add a second reviewer only when you need a specific expert.
Get two approvals for any PR that changes how inventory is read from or written to disk.
One approving review from a maintainer is enough for most PRs.
Do not merge your own PR without an approval, even if branch protection allows it.
Reply to review comments within two working days, or say when you will get to them.
Let the reviewer resolve the threads they opened; resolve a thread yourself only when it was a pure nit you applied.
Reply to every review comment, even if only with `Done` or a link to the fixing commit.
If you disagree with a review comment, explain why with evidence; do not silently ignore it.
Use the re-request review button after you address comments, so the reviewer gets a notice.
Maintainers may close a PR with no activity for 60 days; reopen it when you resume work.
Do not ping reviewers more than once a week on the same PR.
Update the PR description when the approach changes during review; it becomes the merge record.
Add the exact `stock` command line a reviewer can run to see the change.
Leave "Allow edits by maintainers" checked on PRs from forks.
Review dependency-bot PRs like any other PR; do not merge them blind.
If a merged PR breaks `main`, revert first and fix forward in a new PR.
Any maintainer may revert a PR that breaks `main` without waiting for its author.
Link the original PR and the reason in every revert PR description.
When you reland a reverted change, title the PR `Reland: <original title>` and describe what you fixed.
Cross-link related PRs in both descriptions so readers can follow the series.
Do not combine a mass rename with behaviour changes; reviewers cannot see the behaviour change in the noise.
Include before and after numbers in the description for any PR that claims a speedup.
Update user docs in the same PR as the behaviour change, not in a later one.
If you change the sample inventory under `examples/`, explain in the description why the old sample no longer fits.
Do not bump the package version in a feature PR; the release PR does that.
Pair a new contributor's first PR with a maintainer who walks them through review.
Do not put `WIP` in a PR title; use the draft state instead.
Close a PR that another PR supersedes, and link the new one.
For a change over 1000 lines, post a plan in the issue and split it into a numbered series of PRs.
Review for correctness first, then design, then readability; leave style to the formatter.
Check out the branch and run the changed command at least once before you approve a behaviour change.
Check that new tests fail without the change and pass with it.
Say clearly when a comment blocks approval; use "Request changes" only for those.
Use GitHub's suggestion block for small concrete fixes so the author can apply them in one click.
Phrase uncertain points as questions: "Could this run twice on retry?" rather than "This is wrong."
Point out good choices too; a review is not only a list of problems.
Keep review findings to what the PR introduces or worsens; file older problems as issues.
Do not block a PR over a naming preference when the existing name is clear and consistent.
Give a first review within one working day of the request, even if it is partial.
Review large PRs in passes and post comments per pass, rather than one huge batch at the end.
For a PR that changes the stored record shape, check that an old inventory file still loads after the change.
Check quantity arithmetic for off-by-one and sign mistakes, especially in transfers between locations.
Ask how two `stock` processes writing the same inventory at once behave after the change.
Call out any change to the public Python API of `stock`; it needs a deprecation path or a major version.
Question every new runtime dependency; `stock` uses the standard library only.
Check that values read from inventory files are validated before use.
Look for loops that read the whole inventory per item; ask for one pass instead.
Check that README examples still match the commands after the change.
Do not approve a PR you did not read; say "looked at docs only" if that is all you checked.
Attach comments to the exact line they concern, not to the PR conversation tab.
End a review with a short summary that states whether you think the PR is close to merge.
Comment on the code, never on the person; write "this function" instead of "you".
When author and reviewer disagree twice on the same point, bring in a third maintainer.
Accept a follow-up issue for non-blocking improvements instead of growing the PR.
Check that new names use the inventory vocabulary from the glossary: item, SKU, location, movement.
Run every command a PR adds to the README and confirm it works as written.
Open any sample inventory file the PR changes and confirm the numbers add up.
Ask the author to delete code the PR leaves unused rather than keeping it "just in case".
Allow a new TODO only when it links an open issue.
Point out copied blocks of code and ask whether one shared function would be clearer.
Do not ask for an abstraction over two similar call sites; wait for the third.
Do not rerun a failing check more than once without looking at why it failed.
Ask why if a PR skips a CI job that normally runs for the changed paths.
Ask for the source of any binary file a PR adds.
Check that copied third-party code keeps its license notice and is listed in `NOTICE`.
Re-review after the author pushes substantial changes; GitHub dismisses stale approvals on protected branches.
Squash-merge feature PRs so `main` gets one commit per PR.
Use rebase-merge for a PR whose commits were curated to stand alone.
Do not use merge commits on `main`; the repo allows squash and rebase only.
Edit the squash commit message before you merge; remove the list of fixup subjects GitHub adds.
The PR author merges after approval, unless the author is an outside contributor.
Merge only when all required checks are green; never use admin override to skip them.
Use the merge queue when `main` moves fast; do not rebase by hand in a loop.
Do not merge feature PRs during a release freeze; fixes for the release need a maintainer's approval.
Avoid merging risky storage changes late on a Friday when nobody can watch `main`.
Check the base branch before merging; a PR meant for `release/1.4` must not land on `main` by mistake.
Confirm that linked issues closed after merge; close them by hand if the keyword did not match.
Delete the head branch right after merging.
Post in the maintainers channel after you merge a change that alters the public API.
Add a `backport/1.x` label to a merged fix that must reach the maintained release line.
Make backports with `git cherry-pick -x <sha>` so the commit records its source.
Title a backport PR `[1.4] <original title>` and link the original PR.
Backport fixes and security patches only; never backport a new feature.
Note in the backport description every conflict you resolved by hand.
Merge the fix on `main` first; backport only after it has passed CI there.
Keep a backport as small as the fix; do not pull in refactors that the fix happened to sit on.
The author of the original fix owns its backports unless a maintainer takes them over.
Update `.github/CODEOWNERS` in the same PR that adds a new top-level package.
List teams in CODEOWNERS, not single people, so ownership survives holidays.
The storage package and the on-disk format spec need approval from the storage owners.
Workflow files under `.github/workflows/` need approval from a release maintainer.
Remember that the last matching CODEOWNERS pattern wins; put specific paths below general ones.
Do not make one person the owner of `*`; that turns them into a bottleneck.
Split large features into a stack of small PRs, each one reviewable on its own.
Point each stacked PR at the branch below it, and retarget it to `main` after the lower PR merges.
Number stacked PR titles, such as `[2/4] Add location transfer model`, and list the stack in each description.
Merge a stack from the bottom up; never merge an upper PR first.
Each PR in a stack must pass CI on its own base, not only at the top of the stack.
Keep stacks to four PRs or fewer; a deeper stack means the plan needs rework.
Create release tags as annotated tags: `git tag -a v1.5.0 -m "stock 1.5.0"`.
Never move or delete a pushed release tag; cut a new patch version instead.
Tag releases only from a commit that is on `main` or on a `release/*` branch.
Run `git blame` on lines you plan to change and read the commits that wrote them.
Use `git bisect run make check` to find the commit that broke a behaviour.
Never rewrite published history to remove a file; ask a maintainer to rotate the secret and follow the incident steps.
Do not add Git LFS; keep large fixtures out of the repo instead.
Install the pre-commit hooks after you clone with `pre-commit install`.
Keep pre-commit hooks under five seconds; slow checks belong in CI.
Use `git worktree add` to review a PR while you keep your own branch checked out.
Agents must not push, open PRs, or merge unless the person asks for it.
Agents should show the proposed commit message and wait for approval before they commit.
If the current branch is `main`, create a branch before the first commit.
Agents must never amend, squash, or reword commits written by a person.
Agents open PRs as drafts; a person marks them ready.
Say in the PR description when an agent wrote most of the change.
An agent that wrote a change must not be its only reviewer.
Agents keep the diff to the files the task needs and mention any other problems in the summary.
When an agent finishes, it lists the changed files and the checks it ran.
Let the labeler bot add area labels from paths; correct them by hand if they are wrong.
Thank first-time contributors in the first review comment and point them to `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
Outside contributors must accept the contributor agreement before a maintainer reviews the PR.
Keep the first screen of `README.md` to what `stock` is, how to install it, and one short usage example.
The README install section shows `pip install stock` first; source installs go further down.
Do not put roadmap items in the README; link to the milestones page instead.
Limit README badges to build status, latest release, and supported Python versions.
Every command shown in the README must run as written against a fresh checkout.
Order README sections as: overview, install, quick start, concepts, contributing, license.
Describe what `stock` does in plain words; drop adjectives like `blazing`, `powerful`, or `seamless`.
When a README section grows past a screen, move it to `docs/` and leave a one-line link behind.
End the README with the license name and a link to `LICENSE`; never paste the license text inline.
Point contributors to `CONTRIBUTING.md` from the README rather than repeating its steps.
Write user guide pages around tasks, such as `Count a shelf` or `Move items between sites`, not around modules.
One topic per page under `docs/guide/`; split a page when it covers two unrelated tasks.
Start each guide page with what the reader needs before they begin.
After each step in a guide, state what the reader should see next.
Address the reader as `you` in guides; avoid `we` unless you mean the maintainers.
Write docs in the present tense: `stock moves the items`, not `stock will move the items`.
Prefer active voice in docs so the reader knows who does what.
Keep doc paragraphs to four sentences or fewer.
Link a domain word such as `reservation` or `bin` to its glossary entry the first time a page uses it.
Do not document behaviour that has not shipped; open a docs issue to track it instead.
Mark behaviour added in a recent release with a short `New in 1.4` note at the end of the paragraph.
Remove `New in` notes once the version they mention is two minor releases old.
Do not add terminal screenshots to the docs; paste the text so readers can copy and search it.
Link related guide pages to each other at the end of each page under `See also`.
Keep the FAQ to questions users actually asked; cite the issue number next to each entry.
Put recovery steps for a corrupt inventory file on the troubleshooting page, not scattered across guides.
Runnable examples live in `examples/`, one script per scenario, each under a hundred lines.
Each example must run on its own with only `stock` installed; no shared modules between examples.
Examples use the sample inventory in `examples/data/`; never point them at a real warehouse file.
List every example in `examples/README.md` with one sentence on what it shows.
CI runs every example script; a broken example blocks the merge like a broken unit.
Use realistic SKUs such as `BOLT-M6-30` in examples, not `foo` and `bar`.
Write examples for a first-time reader: no one-liners, no chained comprehensions.
Build the docs site locally with `make docs` before you push a docs change.
Treat docs build warnings as failures; fix them in the same PR.
Do not hand-edit pages under `docs/reference/`; they are generated from the source tree.
Add every new docs page to the site navigation in the same PR that creates it.
When you rename a docs page, add a redirect from the old path.
Paste the docs preview link into the PR description for any docs change.
Ship large docs rewrites in their own PR, apart from code changes.
Use relative links between pages in `docs/` so they work in the repo view and on the site.
Never paste a bare URL in prose; give every link descriptive text.
Do not use `here` or `this link` as link text; name the target page.
Run `make linkcheck` after adding external links; replace dead links rather than removing the sentence.
Link to source code with a commit permalink, not a branch, so the line numbers stay valid.
Do not change a heading that other pages link to without updating those anchors.
Link to external sites only for standards and upstream projects; summarise the rest in our own words.
Put one sentence per line in Markdown source so diffs stay small.
Use one `#` heading per page and do not skip heading levels.
Write headings in sentence case: `Moving items`, not `Moving Items`.
Use fenced code blocks with a language tag such as `console` or `python`.
Prefix terminal commands in docs with `$ ` and show results without the prompt.
Keep list items grammatically parallel: all start with a verb or all are nouns.
Use a table only for data with three or more columns; otherwise use a list.
Do not embed raw HTML in Markdown pages unless the docs theme cannot express it.
Run `make mdlint` before you push; fix findings rather than disabling the rule.
Use bold for UI words and warnings only; do not bold whole sentences.
Use a `!!! warning` box only when skipping it could lose inventory data.
Strip trailing whitespace from Markdown files; the editor setup in the repo does this for you.
Name docs files in lowercase with hyphens, such as `moving-items.md`.
Use numbered lists for steps that must happen in order, bullets for everything else.
Wrap file names, commands, and SKU values in backticks in prose.
Write units next to the number with a space: `5 kg`, `12 pcs`.
Draw architecture diagrams in Mermaid inside the Markdown file, not as exported images.
Keep a diagram to about a dozen boxes; split it if it grows larger.
Give every diagram a one-sentence caption that says what to look at.
When you move a module, update any diagram that shows it in the same PR.
Do not use colour alone to carry meaning in diagrams; add labels.
Keep glossary entries in alphabetical order with a one-sentence definition each.
When a PR adds a new domain term, add its glossary entry in the same PR.
Use one word for one idea: `site` always means a physical warehouse, never a storage backend.
Do not mix `item`, `product`, and `article` in docs; `item` is the term.
Write `SKU` in capitals in prose and `sku` only in code.
Record architecture decisions as ADRs in `docs/adr/`, numbered `0001-short-title.md`.
Every ADR has four sections: context, decision, consequences, status.
Do not rewrite an accepted ADR; write a new one that supersedes it and link both ways.
Write an ADR when a change alters the on-disk inventory format or the public Python API.
Keep an ADR to one page; link to the PR or issue for the long discussion.
ADR status is one of `proposed`, `accepted`, `superseded`, or `rejected`.
Keep rejected ADRs in the folder so the same idea is not proposed again without context.
Add each new ADR to `docs/adr/README.md` with its status.
Write comments that explain why the code does something; the code already shows what.
Delete comments that only restate the next statement, such as `# add one to count`.
Write comments as full sentences with a capital letter and a period.
Put a comment on its own line above the code it describes, not at the end of the line.
Do not commit commented-out code; git history keeps the old version.
Do not put author names or initials in comments; git blame records who wrote it.
Do not add `added in March` style notes to comments; they go stale and git records it.
Keep comments neutral: no jokes, sarcasm, or blame toward other code.
When code works around an upstream bug, link the upstream issue in the comment.
A workaround comment states the condition under which the workaround can be removed.
Update or delete a comment in the same commit that changes the code it describes.
Do not leave a comment that is only an issue number; add a short reason next to it.
Name the unit in a comment when the code does not: `# grams, not kilos`.
Do not draw banner comments made of `####` or `====` to divide a file.
If a file needs section comments to be readable, split it into modules.
Write comments in English, even in files that handle localised item names.
Do not write `sorry` or `hack` in comments; say what is non-obvious and why.
State a non-obvious invariant once, next to where it is held, such as `# quantity never drops below reserved`.
Write a TODO as `# TODO(#123): short reason`, always with an issue number.
Do not add a TODO without an open issue that tracks it.
When you close an issue, remove every TODO that cites it.
Use `TODO` only; do not add `FIXME`, `XXX`, or `HACK` markers.
A PR may add at most two new TODOs; more means the work is not done.
Before a release, review every TODO added since the last tag and either fix it or move it to an issue.
A TODO says what to do next, not just that something is wrong.
Every `# noqa` suppression carries a short reason after it.
Suppress a single lint rule by code, never all rules on a line.
Keep functions short enough to read without scrolling; split them when they pass about forty lines.
A function does one job; if you need two sentences to say what it does, split it.
Do not nest blocks more than three levels deep; extract a function or return early.
Return early for the empty or trivial case so the main path stays at the top level of the function.
Put guard clauses at the top of a function, before any real work starts.
Do not write `else` after a branch that returns.
Prefer a plain loop over a clever one-liner when the one-liner needs a second read.
Use a comprehension for a single map or filter; use a loop when it needs two `for` clauses or a nested condition.
Do not nest walrus assignments inside comprehensions or conditions.
Use a conditional expression only for a simple choice between two values; never chain them.
Avoid double negatives in names and conditions, such as `if not is_not_empty`.
Write conditions in the positive form when you can: `if in_stock` rather than `if not out_of_stock`.
Do not mutate a function argument the caller passed in; build and return a new value.
Do not use `map` with `lambda`; use a comprehension or a loop.
Break a chain of more than three method calls into named intermediate values.
Name intermediate results when a single expression computes more than one idea.
Keep paired operations symmetric: if `reserve` takes a location, `release` takes one too.
Do not index into nested structures more than two levels in one expression; unpack them first.
Never address record fields by position when they have names.
Use one-letter names only in comprehensions and loops of three lines or fewer.
Spell names out: `quantity`, not `qty`; `location`, not `loc`.
The only accepted abbreviation in names is `sku`, because the domain uses it.
Name collections in the plural and single values in the singular.
Do not put the container kind into a name: `items`, not `item_list`.
Put the public functions of a module at the top and the private ones below them.
Prefix module-private names with one underscore; do not use two.
Keep code that changes together in the same module, grouped by feature, not by kind.
Do not create `utils.py` or `misc.py`; give each shared function a home named after its subject.
Split a module once it holds more than one main concept or passes about four hundred lines of code.
Order functions so that a caller appears above the functions it calls.
Do not start a module with a license header; the repo `LICENSE` covers every file.
Delete unused functions and branches instead of keeping them for later.
Keep `__init__.py` files nearly empty; re-expose only the names users call.
Name a module after the one concept it holds, such as `reservation.py`.
Keep the domain model modules free of disk access and terminal handling.
Keep command modules thin: parse input, call the domain layer, render the result.
Do not let one class own items, locations, and movements at once; split it by concept.
Within a class, order members as: class attributes, init, public methods, private methods.
Avoid functions defined inside functions unless they are closures that need the outer scope.
Do not nest classes inside classes; put each at module level.
Write code so a reviewer can understand a function without opening three other files.
Move code and change code in separate commits so the diff of the change stays readable.
Do not reformat code you did not otherwise change in the same PR.
Do not keep module-level mutable state; pass state in explicitly.
Prefer functions that take values and return values over ones that change shared objects.
A lookup that answers a question about inventory must not change anything.
Use `match` only when it reads more clearly than an `if` chain of three or more branches.
Pass a named function as a sort key when the key needs more than one attribute.
Compare quantities with `== 0` explicitly; do not rely on truthiness of numbers.
Check for `None` with `is None`, never with `== None` or truthiness when zero is a valid value.
Write range checks as `low <= qty <= high`, not as two separate comparisons.
Use an enum for a closed set of values such as movement kinds, not free strings.
If a function takes more than five parameters, group the related ones into an object.
Put the main subject first in parameter lists: `move(item, source, target)`.
Do not shadow built-in names such as `id`, `list`, `type`, or `input`.
Do not prefix names with their kind, such as `str_name` or `lst_items`.
Use domain words in code: `reorder_point`, `on_hand`, `reserved`, matching the glossary.
Avoid vague names such as `data`, `info`, `obj`, and `tmp` outside throwaway scopes.
Name counts with a `_count` suffix and quantities with no suffix: `item_count`, `quantity`.
Put the unit in a name when the value has one: `weight_grams`, `lead_days`.
Name identifiers with an `_id` suffix so they are not mistaken for full records.
Separate the steps of a function with single blank lines; never use two inside a function.
Do not align values in columns with extra spaces; it makes later diffs noisy.
Use trailing commas in multi-line collections so adding an entry changes one line.
Prefer explicit arguments over reading values from a shared object deep in the call chain.
Keep refactors for readability in their own PR with no behaviour change.
If a reviewer asks what a line does, rewrite the line rather than adding a comment.
Wait for the third copy of a pattern before you extract a shared function.
Remove a function that only forwards to another function with the same arguments.
Keep class hierarchies to two levels; prefer composition beyond that.
Do not use metaclasses or `__getattr__` tricks in application code.
Never monkeypatch library objects at runtime in `stock` itself.
Do not add attributes to objects with `setattr` from computed names.
Do not add catch-all parameters to a function unless it truly forwards them to another call.
The API reference covers only public names; private modules stay out of it.
Use American English spelling in docs and comments, such as `color` and `center`.
Spell out numbers below ten in prose and use digits for quantities and versions.
Do not use internal shorthand in user docs; write `reservation` instead of `resv`.
Show command examples against the sample inventory so readers get the same results.
Keep command examples free of results inside the same block so readers can copy them directly.
Ask a docs owner from `CODEOWNERS` to review any change under `docs/guide/`.
Write an upgrade guide page for every release that changes the on-disk format.
Upgrade guides list exact steps in order, with a backup step first.
Document known limits, such as the largest tested inventory size, on one page.
Link the ADR from the guide page whose behaviour it explains.
Keep `CONTRIBUTING.md` to setup, workflow, and review; move deep topics into `docs/dev/`.
Keep `docs/dev/architecture.md` current; update it when a layer gains or loses a module.
Give every image in the docs alt text that says what it shows.
Do not use emoji in docs, comments, or commit messages.
Use `allowlist` and `denylist`, not older terms with the same meaning.
When you change a workflow described in this file, update this file in the same PR.
Stream rows from the backend one at a time; do not load the whole inventory into memory to answer a question about one SKU.
Avoid nested loops over items and locations. Build a lookup by SKU first, then walk the movements once.
Keep an in-memory index keyed by SKU when a command touches more than a handful of items.
Measure before you optimise. Attach the numbers from the profiler to the PR, not a guess.
Profile a slow command with `python -m cProfile -s cumtime -m stock report` and share the top twenty rows.
Benchmarks run against the 100k-item fixture, not the ten-item sample used in docs.
Keep the benchmark job separate from the main CI job so a slow runner does not block merges.
A PR that slows a tracked benchmark by more than 10% needs a note in the description that says why.
Do not connect to the backend until a command actually reads or writes inventory.
Defer loading of report-only modules until the report command runs.
Return generators from read paths that can yield many rows, for example `iter_movements()`.
If a caller needs to walk rows twice, materialise them once with `list()` at the call site, not inside the backend.
Group writes into one transaction per command, not one per item.
Commit large bulk loads in batches of about 1000 rows so a crash loses at most one batch.
Use `executemany` for bulk inserts into SQLite instead of a Python loop of `execute` calls.
Add an SQLite index for every column that a command filters on, and name it after the column.
Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on any new SQL that runs per item and paste the plan in the PR.
Fetch quantities for all requested SKUs in one query; never query per SKU inside a loop.
Drop any cached quantity for a SKU in the same code path that writes a movement for it.
Key caches on the full lookup identity, such as `(sku, location)`, never on a partial key.
Use `functools.lru_cache` only on pure functions of immutable inputs.
Do not put `lru_cache` on instance methods; it keeps every instance alive for the life of the process.
Give every cache a size bound. An unbounded dict keyed by SKU grows with the warehouse.
Write the data file through a temp file in the same folder, flush, fsync, then rename it over the target.
Create the temp file next to the target, not in the system temp folder, so the rename stays on one filesystem.
After the rename, fsync the parent folder so the new directory entry survives a power loss.
A reader must never see a half-written data file. If you cannot make a write atomic, do not ship it.
Remove the temp file if the write does not complete; leave no `.tmp` files behind in the data folder.
Keep the critical section short: compute the new state first, then lock, re-read, apply, and write.
Never hold the data lock while waiting for the person to answer a prompt.
Re-read the current state after you take the lock; the copy you read before may be stale.
Each backend owns its own locking story. Callers must not lock the file from outside the backend.
Run SQLite in WAL mode so a long report does not block a concurrent `stock add`.
Set a busy wait on SQLite connections so two CLI runs queue instead of failing at once.
Keep SQLite write transactions short; start them with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for read-modify-write.
Design every bulk command so a crash mid-batch leaves the data in the state before or after a whole batch.
The movement ledger is the source of truth; on-hand quantities must be rebuildable by replaying it.
Append to the ledger; never rewrite earlier movements to correct a mistake. Add a reversing movement.
Add a crash test for each new write path: kill the process between steps and check the file still loads.
Do not use sleeps to wait for a lock in tests; use a barrier or an event so the test is fast and stable.
Cover concurrent writers with a test that runs two processes against one data file.
Do not add threads to speed up a command. The CLI is single-threaded by design and the storage layer assumes it.
If a report truly needs parallel work, use a process pool over read-only snapshots and merge the results.
Large reports read from a snapshot taken under the lock, then release the lock before they format rows.
Write report rows as they are produced; do not build the full report as one big string.
Pass a file object to `csv.writer` and write row by row for exports; never join rows in memory first.
Chunk reports over 50k rows by location so peak memory stays flat.
A command on the 100k-item fixture must stay under 200 MB of resident memory.
Use `tracemalloc` to find memory growth; attach the top allocation sites to the PR.
Do not copy row dicts to tweak one field; build the new value at the point of use.
Avoid `copy.deepcopy` on inventory state; it is slow on large trees and hides shared-state bugs.
Sort once at the edge of the report. Do not sort intermediate lists that nobody reads in order.
Use `heapq.nsmallest` or `heapq.nlargest` for top-N lists instead of sorting the whole inventory.
Use `bisect` on sorted SKU lists for range lookups rather than linear scans.
Use a set for membership checks against many SKUs; a list check is linear each call.
Use `collections.Counter` or a dict to sum quantities per key in one pass.
Use `Decimal` for unit costs and keep the cost of conversions out of inner loops.
Compile regexes used per row once at module level, not inside the loop.
Build strings with `''.join(parts)`, never with `+=` in a loop.
Do not optimise code that runs once per command on a few items; readable beats fast there.
State in the PR how the change behaves at 10, 10k, and 1M items when it touches a read path.
Tag pull requests that change performance with the `perf` label so the benchmark job runs.
Run local benchmarks with `make bench`; it pins the fixture and warms the cache before measuring.
Run each benchmark at least five rounds and report the median, not the best run.
Compare benchmark numbers only from the same machine and the same Python build.
Record a baseline on `main` before you measure your branch; numbers from last month are not a baseline.
Use `timeit` for micro-benchmarks of a single function and keep them out of the main suite.
Do not put speed checks in the unit suite; they flake on shared runners.
Report both warm and cold runs for startup changes; the cold run is what people feel.
For deep call stacks, render a flame graph with `py-spy record` and link the SVG in the PR.
The hot paths are quantity lookup, movement append, and the on-hand report. Treat changes there with extra care.
In tight loops, bind repeated attribute lookups to a local name before the loop.
Do not reach for regex where `str.startswith` or `str.split` will do.
Prefer `sum`, `min`, `max`, `any`, and `all` over hand-written loops; they run in C.
Use comprehensions for row transforms; they are as fast as `map` and easier to read.
Do not keep inventory state in module globals; it leaks between commands in long-lived callers.
Remember that `stock` is also a library. A caller may run thousands of operations in one process, so no per-call leaks.
Close backend connections at the end of each operation scope; use a context manager.
Wrap every acquired resource, such as a lock, a connection, or a temp file, in a `with` block.
On Ctrl-C mid-write, finish or roll back the current batch; never leave a half-applied batch.
Treat a lock file older than its owning process as stale; check the PID in it before you break it.
Write the owner PID into the lock file so a stale lock can be detected and reported.
Never delete a lock held by a live process, even if the wait is long.
`fcntl` locks do not exist on Windows; keep the platform switch inside the lock module only.
All file locking lives in one module. Do not call `fcntl` or `msvcrt` from anywhere else.
Network filesystems break advisory locks; the docs must say that the data folder must be on a local disk.
The design assumes one writer at a time per data file. Do not add code paths that write without the lock.
Plain reads of the SQLite backend do not take the file lock; WAL gives them a consistent view.
The CSV backend has no WAL, so readers take a shared lock too.
Keep a checksum next to each CSV data file and check it on load to catch torn writes.
Copy the data file aside before a schema migration and keep the copy until the migration commits.
Run each schema migration inside one transaction so a crash leaves the old schema intact.
Test every migration against the 100k-item fixture and note how long it takes in the PR.
Do not run `VACUUM` automatically; offer it as `stock compact` so people choose when to pay for it.
Compaction folds old movements into an opening balance; it must keep totals per SKU exactly equal.
After compaction, replay the ledger and compare on-hand totals before you replace the old file.
The ledger grows forever unless compacted; keep reads that walk it rare and bounded.
Keep a materialised on-hand table updated in the same transaction as each movement, so reads stay O(1).
Provide `stock rebuild` to recompute on-hand from the ledger when the two disagree.
Run the on-hand versus ledger check in CI against every fixture.
Applying the same movement batch twice must not double the quantities; check the batch id first.
Give each bulk load a batch id and store it, so a retried load can skip work that already landed.
Make every write command safe to retry after a crash without manual cleanup.
Do not use `mmap` on the data files; it complicates locking and crash safety for little gain.
Use buffered writes for exports and flush once at the end; unbuffered writes are slow on big files.
Flush and fsync the temp file before the rename. A rename of unflushed data can produce an empty file after a crash.
Rename is atomic on POSIX only within one filesystem; keep the temp file in the target folder.
On Windows a rename fails if the target is open; retry a few rounds with a short back-off.
Check that a write path leaves the old file intact when the disk fills mid-write.
Before a large export, compare the expected size with free space and stop early if it will not fit.
Library calls that can return many rows take a `limit` and return a cursor for the next page.
Page cursors are based on SKU order, not on offsets, so inserts between pages do not skip rows.
Do not page with `OFFSET` in SQL on large tables; seek on the last seen key instead.
Answer `stock count` with a single aggregate query, not by fetching rows and counting in Python.
Push sums and group-bys into SQL for the SQLite backend; Python loops over rows are the fallback.
A query pushed into SQL must give the same totals as the Python fallback used by the CSV backend.
Keep one shared test table that runs every aggregate on every backend and compares the totals.
The in-memory backend is for tests and must stay fast; do not add persistence hooks to it.
Generate the large fixture with `make fixtures`; do not commit files over 5 MB to the repo.
Seed the fixture generator so every run produces the same rows and benchmarks stay comparable.
Document known slow paths in `docs/performance.md` with the size where they start to hurt.
Ask reporters of slow runs for item count, backend kind, and the profiler output.
Reproduce a reported slowdown at the reported size before you change any code.
Do not tune the garbage collector in the CLI; fix the allocation pattern instead.
SKU strings repeat across millions of movements; intern them when loading large ledgers.
Do not add pandas or numpy to speed up reports; the package stays standard library only.
Bound every lock wait; a command must not hang forever behind a stuck writer.
When a lock wait gives up, name the PID that holds the lock so the person can check it.
Locks are not re-entrant. Do not take the data lock again inside code that already holds it.
Concurrency tests use a fresh temp folder per case so stale locks from one case never leak into the next.
Commands that only read must open the SQLite file read-only, so they can never take a write lock by accident.
Each command declares up front whether it writes; the dispatcher takes the lock only for writers.
A read command must never touch the data file on disk, not even to update a cache or a counter.
If you cache derived data on disk, key it on the data file size and inode, and drop it when either changes.
Do not add an on-disk cache without a measured win of at least 2x on the large fixture.
Derived cache files live under `.stock-cache/` and stay out of git.
Count the cost of building a cache in the benchmark; a cache that pays off only on the third run is a loss for a CLI.
Memoise lookups for the duration of one command run through a plain dict passed down, not a hidden global.
Parse each data row once. Pass parsed values down; do not re-parse the raw row in later steps.
Convert quantity and cost strings to numbers at the backend boundary, once per row.
`csv.DictReader` is slower than `csv.reader`; use the plain reader in hot loops and map columns by index.
Resolve column positions from the header row once, before the loop over data rows.
Do not convert columns that the current command does not read.
Stop scanning as soon as the answer is known; `any()` over a generator beats building a list first.
Filter by location or SKU prefix in the backend query, not after loading all rows.
Support SKU prefix filters with an index-friendly range query, `sku >= 'AB' AND sku < 'AC'`.
Avoid `LIKE '%x%'` on large tables; it forces a full scan. Offer prefix search instead.
Case-fold SKUs once when they are written, so lookups never need to fold both sides.
Normalise SKU and location values on write, so reads stay simple and fast.
The reorder report walks on-hand rows once and compares against reorder points in the same pass.
Join on-hand with reorder points in SQL for the SQLite backend instead of two Python passes.
Do not recompute the full valuation report when one item changes; update the affected totals.
Valuation over the whole ledger is the slowest report; warn reviewers when a change touches it.
Keep FIFO cost layers in a deque per SKU so consumption pops from the left in O(1).
Never call `list.pop(0)` in a loop; use `collections.deque`.
Use `dict.setdefault` or `defaultdict` to group rows; avoid a membership check then a second lookup.
Bind `rows.append` to a local in loops that run over 100k rows.
Do not walk location trees with recursion; deep trees hit the recursion limit. Use an explicit stack.
Precompute the location tree once per run; do not walk parent links for every movement.
Moving many items between locations is one ledger batch, not one command run per item.
Expose bulk variants in the library API, `add_many()`, so callers do not loop over the single-item call.
Bulk calls apply exactly the same validation as single calls; speed is not a reason to skip checks.
Validate input before you take the lock, so invalid input never holds up other writers.
Do expensive pure work, such as parsing a large input file, before taking the write lock.
A single quantity change must not rewrite the whole CSV file when an append will do.
The CSV backend appends movements and rewrites the on-hand file only at compaction.
Rewrite the on-hand CSV only when the pending deltas pass a size threshold, then fold them in.
Use `synchronous=NORMAL` with WAL; it keeps durability across process crashes at lower cost.
Let SQLite checkpoint the WAL on its own; do not force checkpoints after each write.
Set SQLite pragmas in one place when the connection is made, never ad hoc in commands.
Use one SQLite connection per command run; opening a new one per query is slow.
Reuse the same SQL text for repeated queries so SQLite can reuse its prepared statement cache.
For large set operations on SKUs, load them into a temp table and join, rather than a giant `IN` list.
Keep `IN (...)` lists under 500 items; chunk larger lists.
Avoid a custom row factory in hot paths; plain tuples are faster than `sqlite3.Row`.
Use `fetchmany(1000)` in loops over large result sets rather than `fetchall()`.
Let SQL sort large result sets with an index; sorting in Python after `fetchall()` doubles memory.
Exports come out in SKU order so diffs between two exports stay small.
A long export writes to a temp file and renames on success, so a broken export never overwrites a good one.
Offer gzip for exports over 50 MB through the `.gz` suffix on the target name.
Use gzip level 6 for exports; level 9 costs much more and saves little.
Code on cold paths, such as `stock init`, can trade speed for clarity.
Modules must do no work when they load: no file reads, no network, no regex compilation of large tables.
The console entry point stays thin; it dispatches and lets each command load what it needs.
Discover backend plugins through entry points only when a non-default backend is asked for.
`stock` is I/O bound on small data and CPU bound on large ledgers; profile before you assume either.
Benchmarks run on the oldest supported Python as well as the newest; a win on one can be a loss on the other.
Do not add C extensions or compiled modules for speed; pure Python keeps install trivial.
Fix the algorithm before you micro-tune; a better loop shape beats local name tricks.
If a perf change makes the code hard to follow and the win is under 10%, revert it.
Mark a non-obvious speed trick with a short comment that names the benchmark it serves.
Benchmark results go to `bench/results/` as CSV, one row per run, and are not committed.

Document the durability promise in `docs/storage.md`: a completed command survives a crash; an interrupted one leaves no trace.
Use the fault-injection hook in the write path to simulate a crash between fsync and rename in tests.
Use `dict.get` with a default for lookups in hot loops rather than a membership check followed by indexing.
Each benchmark models one user action, such as an on-hand report over 100k items, and says so in its title.
Keep a ledger movement row small: SKU, location, delta, batch id, and nothing derived.
Do not store values in the ledger that can be computed from other fields; they drift and bloat the file.
Fixture data uses obviously fake credentials such as `hunter2-not-real`; keep it that way.
When you paste command output into an issue or PR, redact anything that looks like a token or a password.
If a task needs a credential you do not have, stop and ask the maintainer instead of inventing a placeholder.
Never write secret values into reports, exported files, or the inventory ledger.

Resolve every export target and check it stays inside the chosen output folder before you write.
Reject output names that contain `..` segments or a drive letter.

Nightly builds are CI artifacts only; never publish them to PyPI.

Do not use `[skip ci]` in commit messages on PR branches.
macOS runners are slow; keep the macOS cells to the oldest and newest Python only.
Jobs must write scratch data under the runner temp folder, never into the checkout.
Delete workflow runs and caches older than 30 days with the scheduled cleanup job.
The required checks are `lint`, `test`, `build`, and `docs`; adding one needs maintainer agreement.
Schedule cron jobs at an odd minute, e.g. `17 3 * * *`, to avoid the top-of-hour queue.
Run the lint job first and make the test matrix depend on it, so style breaks fail fast and cheap.
Tests in CI must not reach the network; anything that needs it lives in the nightly job.
Retry only steps that hit outside services, such as package downloads, and never the test step.
Keep job output short; send long reports to artifacts rather than the job page.
Changes under `.github/` need review from a member of the `maintainers` team.
A fork must be able to run the PR workflow with no secrets at all.
Pin the ruff version in `pyproject.toml` dev extras and in pre-commit; bump both together.
Run `pre-commit autoupdate` once a month in a separate PR.
Use ruff as the only linter and formatter; do not add flake8, isort, black, or pylint.
Every `# noqa` names the rule code, e.g. `# noqa: E741`; a bare `noqa` fails review.
Add a short reason after a `noqa` code when the reason is not obvious from the code.
Do not add a rule to the global ignore list to silence one file; use a per-file ignore.
Keep per-file ignores in `pyproject.toml`, sorted by path.
Enable new ruff rule sets in a dedicated PR that also fixes every finding.
Keep ruff preview rules off on `main`; try them on a branch first.
Do not mix mass reformatting with behaviour changes in one PR.
Add the commit SHA of a mass reformat to `.git-blame-ignore-revs`.
Keep the ruff `C901` limit at 10; split a function that goes over it instead of raising the limit.
Keep the `S` (bandit) rule set on for `src/`; it may be off for the tests folder only.
Keep the `UP` rules on and target the oldest supported Python version.
Run `mdformat` on `docs/` and `README.md`; keep wrap off so diffs stay small.
Keep `pyproject.toml` sections in the order build-system, project, dependencies, tool.
Run `codespell` on docs and source; add real words to `.codespell-ignore`, not to each file.
Strip trailing spaces and end every file with a single newline; the hook does this for you.
Do not commit editor folders such as `.vscode/` or `.idea/`.
If you think a lint rule is wrong for this codebase, open an issue; do not disable it in passing.
Triage new issues every Monday; every issue gets a type label and a priority label within a week.
Use exactly one type label per issue: `bug`, `feature`, `docs`, `question`, or `chore`.
Add area labels such as `area/storage`, `area/cli`, or `area/reports` so owners can filter.
Use `p0` for data loss, `p1` for broken commands with no workaround, `p2` for the rest.
A `p0` issue blocks the next release and gets an owner the same day.
Ask for the `stock` version, Python version, OS, and the exact command before you label a bug confirmed.
Label an issue `needs-repro` when you cannot reproduce it, and say what you tried.
Reduce a reported bug to the smallest inventory file and command that shows it before you fix it.
Add `confirmed` only after you reproduce the bug on the latest release or `main`.
Close duplicates with a link to the original and the `duplicate` label; copy any new details over.
Search open and closed issues before you file a new one.
Mark issues with no reply from the reporter for 30 days as `stale`; close them after 14 more days.
Never auto-close issues labelled `confirmed`, `p0`, or `security`.
Label an issue `good first issue` only if it has a clear scope, the files to touch, and a test to write.
Use `contributions welcome` for issues maintainers agree on but will not work on soon.
Put an issue in a milestone only when someone has committed to ship it in that version.
Assign yourself before you start work so no one else starts the same fix.
If you stop work on an issue, unassign yourself and leave a note on where you got to.
Move usage questions to GitHub Discussions; keep issues for bugs and agreed work.
Discuss a new feature in an issue before anyone opens a PR for it.
Ask for the real use case behind a feature request; the requested design is often not the best one.
Close with `wontfix` and one sentence of reason; do not leave rejected ideas open.
Label a bug `regression` when it worked in an earlier release, and name that release.
For a regression, run `git bisect` between the last good tag and `main` and post the bad commit.
Keep the issue forms in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; every bug form asks for the exact command and version.
Turn off blank issues; route people to a form or to Discussions.
Thank the reporter, stay polite, and do not argue in issues; move long design debates to a call.
Close the issue from the PR with `Fixes #123`, not by hand.
When a reporter says a fix did not work, reopen the issue rather than filing a new one.
Pin at most three issues; keep the known-problems issue pinned during a release candidate.
Lock closed issues after 90 days so new reports land in new issues.
Keep the roadmap in a GitHub project board, not in the issue tracker labels.
Split large features into a parent issue with a task list of child issues.
Edit vague issue titles into a short statement of the problem, e.g. `count ignores reserved units`.
Add an `os/windows` or `os/macos` label when a bug only shows on one platform.
Label issues caused by a tool or Python itself `upstream` and link the upstream report.
Each area label has an owner listed in `CODEOWNERS`; they triage that label first.
Answer every new issue within five working days, even if the answer is only that it is queued.
Ask reporters to share redacted inventory samples only; never ask for their real supplier data.
Remove attachments that contain personal or supplier data and tell the reporter why.
Link every PR to an issue; only small typo fixes may skip this.
Ping a PR author after 14 days without reply and close the PR after 30 more days.
Do not review draft PRs unless the author asks a direct question.
Approve CI runs for first-time contributors after a quick read of the workflow changes.
Do not take the `hacktoberfest` label; low-effort PRs get closed without review.
Do not reply to bot comments in issues; resolve or dismiss them.
Review the open-issue count and median age at each release retro.
Use `needs-info` when you are waiting for the reporter; the stale timer only runs on this label.
Anyone may ask to reopen a closed issue with new evidence; maintainers decide.
If a bug report is caused by unclear docs, fix the docs and label the issue `docs`.
When two issues share a root cause, link them both ways before you fix either.
Keep the label set in `.github/labels.yml` and sync it with the labels workflow; do not edit labels in the web UI.
When an agent triages, it may suggest labels in a comment but must not close or lock issues.
Use the `release-blocker` label only with maintainer agreement and a target version.
For performance reports, ask for item count, location count, and the backend in use.
After a fix ships, comment on the issue with the version that contains it.
Hide `+1` comments as off-topic and point people to the reaction button.
When closing a duplicate, add the reporter's words to the original issue title or body so search finds it.
Before a long absence, reassign your `p0` and `p1` issues to another maintainer.
Treat everything reachable from `stock` without an underscore as public API; anything under `stock._internal` may change in any release.
Do not reorder parameters of a public call, even when the new order reads better.
If a reorder is unavoidable, ship a compatibility shim and a regression check that exercises the old call pattern.
Deprecate a public name for at least one minor release before removing it.
Remove deprecated public names only in a major release.
Follow semantic versioning for the library surface: patch for fixes, minor for additions, major for breaks.
Treat the human-readable report layout as unstable; scripts should read the machine-readable export instead.
Treat the CSV export column set and order as a public contract; add columns only at the end.
