Never rename an export column in a minor release; add the new column and deprecate the old one.
Return tuples from public queries so callers cannot mutate a result that stock may cache.
Return `types.MappingProxyType` when exposing an internal mapping, never the dict itself.
Copy mutable collections that callers pass in before keeping them on a model.
Return an iterator from queries that can yield more than a few thousand rows; offer a list form only if a caller needs it.
State in the reference docs when a returned iterable is single-pass.
Page through item listings with an opaque cursor, not a numeric offset, so inserts do not shift pages.
Callers must not parse cursors; keep their shape private so it can change freely.
Give every listing a deterministic order, with SKU as the final tie-breaker.
Cap page size at 500 items and clamp larger requests instead of honouring them.
Represent counted quantities as `int` in the smallest unit; never store fractional pieces.
Represent weighed or measured quantities as `Decimal`, never `float`.
Keep unit prices and stock values as `Decimal` from input to report; convert only at the display edge.
Pair every price with an ISO 4217 currency code; a bare number is not a price.
Do not add values of different currencies; reject the operation instead of guessing a rate.
Round money with `ROUND_HALF_EVEN` at two places unless the currency defines another exponent.
Round once, at the boundary where a value leaves stock; keep full precision in between.
Keep the unit of measure next to every measured quantity; never infer it from the item name.
Use UN/CEFACT unit codes such as `KGM`, `MTR` and `EA` as the canonical unit identifiers.
Keep unit conversion factors in one table in `stock/units.py`; callers never multiply by magic numbers.
Do not convert units silently when adding two quantities; require the caller to convert first.
Allow negative on-hand counts only when the location opts in; otherwise reject the movement.
Use the SKU as the identity of an item; names and descriptions may change, the SKU may not.
Normalise SKUs to upper case on input and compare them only in normalised form.
Accept SKUs made of A-Z, 0-9, dash and dot only; reject anything else at the boundary.
Write location codes as `WAREHOUSE/AISLE/BIN`, for example `MAIN/A03/B12`.
Expose identifiers as strings in the public API, even when a backend keeps them as integers.
Identify each stock movement with a UUID4 so movements from two machines never collide.
Never reuse the identifier of a deleted item or movement.
Do not promise callers that identifiers increase; sort by the recorded sequence field instead.
Give models value equality on their fields; two items with the same SKU and fields compare equal.
Property access must never touch the backend; use an explicit method for anything that reads storage.
Make mutating methods return `None` or the new record, never both kinds depending on the input.
Return one shape per function; do not return a list for many results and a single object for one.
Return `None` from a lookup that finds nothing; reserve signalling for real faults.
Return an empty tuple, not `None`, when a listing has no rows.
Never use `-1` or `0` as a sentinel for an unknown quantity; use `None`.
Prefer an explicit argument over reading ambient state inside a library call.
Library code never asks the user a question; the CLI asks, then passes the answer in.
The CLI may use only the public library surface, so every CLI feature is also usable from Python.
Do not let callers register backends by mutating a module-level dict; expose a registration call.
Discover third-party backends through the `stock.backends` entry-point group.
Load entry-point plugins lazily, on first use, so startup stays fast.
Stamp every data file with a schema version and refuse to write to a file from a newer schema.
Write schema migrations forward-only; a downgrade means reading an older backup.
Make each migration step idempotent so a run that stops halfway can simply run again.
Do not remove or rename a persisted field; add a new one and keep reading the old one.
Do not change a default value in a way that alters the behaviour of existing inventories.
Never change the stored value of an enum member; add a new member instead.
Back movement kinds with `enum.Enum` whose values are short lower-case strings like `receive` and `issue`.
When reading data written by a newer version, keep unknown movement kinds as opaque values instead of dropping the row.
Model a reservation as its own record with a quantity and a holder; never lower on-hand stock to reserve it.
Do not persist any value the library can derive from the movement history.
Treat the movement history as append-only; correct a mistake with a reversing movement, not an edit.
Give each reversing movement a link to the movement it cancels.
Do not batch writes behind the caller's back; offer an explicit batch call instead.
Make a batch of movements apply in full or not at all.
Return the resulting balance from a movement call so the caller does not need a second read.
Keep reorder and valuation calculations pure: inputs in, result out, no backend access.
Keep public calls to five parameters or fewer; group related values into a model when you need more.
Accept any iterable of items as input, and return a concrete tuple as output.
Do not let one parameter accept both a SKU and a location code; give each its own parameter.
Pass movement kinds as enum members in library code; parse strings only at the CLI edge.
Parse and validate user input once, at the edge; inner layers trust their inputs.
Whatever the library writes it must be able to read back without loss.
For every export format, keep a round-trip check: export, read back, compare equal.
Write numbers in data files with a dot as the decimal separator, whatever the user's locale is.
Apply locale-aware number formatting only in human-readable reports.
Group thousands in report quantities, for example `12,480`, but never in exported data.
Show a zero quantity as `0`, never as a blank cell or a dash.
Show an unknown quantity as `-` in reports so it is not confused with zero.
Show unit costs with the full currency precision in reports; truncate nothing.
Show percentages in reports with one decimal place, for example `12.5%`.
Never let a quantity or price render in scientific notation; format `Decimal` values with `:f`.
Ask a maintainer to review any change that adds, removes or alters a public name.
List every public API change in the PR description under a separate heading.
Run `make api-check` after you touch the public surface; it compares exported names with the last release.
Label a PR `breaking` when it changes a public signature, return shape or persisted field.
Never merge a breaking change into a patch release branch.
Every breaking change ships with a migration note in `docs/upgrading.md`.
Show the before and after call in each upgrade note, side by side.
Put unstable features under `stock.experimental`; they carry no compatibility promise.
Move a feature out of `stock.experimental` only after one release with no reported design problems.
Core modules must not depend on `stock.experimental`.
Mark every experimental page in the docs with a visible "Experimental" banner.
Treat the minimum supported Python version as part of the contract; lift it only in a minor release with notice.
Do not reach into the private attributes of another stock module, even from inside the package.
Prefix module-level names that callers should not use with a single underscore.
Do not re-export names from third-party packages as part of the stock surface.
Accept the narrowest input that works; widening later is compatible, narrowing is not.
Return the narrowest result shape you can; adding fields later is compatible, removing them is not.
Use one word for one concept across the whole API: an `item` is never also a `product` or an `article`.
Check new names against the glossary in `docs/glossary.md` before you add them to the API.
Use `quantity` for amounts in the API; do not mix in `qty`, `amount` or `count`.
Use `on_hand` for physical stock and `available` for stock that is free to promise.
Say `location` in the API and in user text; `bin`, `slot` and `shelf` are parts of a location code only.
Say `supplier`, not `vendor`, everywhere a party that delivers stock is meant.
Spell out words in public names; `warehouse`, not `wh`.
Document the sort order of every public listing and keep it stable across releases.
The library must never make network calls unless the caller chose a remote backend.
State in the reference docs whether each public object is safe to share between threads.
Assume a single writer per data file; document the locking that enforces it.
Hold the data file lock only for the write itself, never across user prompts.
Let callers pass an idempotency key with a movement so a retried receipt is not counted twice.
Compare measured quantities only after both are in the same unit.
Never truncate a SKU, name or note silently; reject values that exceed the stored width.
Cap item names at 120 code points and say so in the reference docs.
Keep free-text notes opaque: store, return and export them exactly as given.
Ask the user to confirm before any action that deletes items, locations or history.
Name the exact target in a confirmation, for example `Delete location MAIN/A03/B12 and its 14 items?`.
Include the number of affected records in every confirmation prompt.
Make "no" the default answer of every destructive confirmation: `[y/N]`.
For irreversible bulk deletes, ask the user to type the warehouse code instead of answering y.
Never ask for confirmation before a read-only action.
When there is no terminal to ask, refuse a destructive action rather than assume yes.
Write user-facing text in sentence case: `Stock moved`, not `Stock Moved`.
Do not use exclamation marks in user-facing text.
Keep the tone neutral and calm; state facts, do not say sorry or celebrate.
Address the user as "you" and refer to the tool as "stock", never as "we" or "I".
Describe the state of things in present tense: `3 items are below the reorder point`.
Confirm a finished action in past tense: `Received 40 EA of BOLT-M6 at MAIN/A03/B12`.
Start an instruction to the user with a verb: `Run stock count to rebuild balances.`
Use the same verb for the same action everywhere: receive, issue, move, adjust, count.
Do not say "transfer" in one place and "move" in another for the same action.
Say "adjust" for a manual correction and "count" for a physical count; never swap them.
Pluralise nouns by count: `1 item`, `2 items`, `0 items`.
Never write `item(s)`; compute the right plural.
Write counts as digits in user text, even small ones: `3 locations`, not `three locations`.
Always show a measured quantity with its unit: `12.5 KGM`, never a bare `12.5`.
Show SKUs exactly as stored, in upper case, without added punctuation around them.
Show the full location code in user text; do not shorten `MAIN/A03/B12` to `B12`.
Keep report column headings to one or two words: `SKU`, `Location`, `On hand`, `Reserved`.
Put the unit or currency in the heading, not in every cell: `Value (EUR)`.
Right-align numeric columns in reports and left-align text columns.
Put a totals row at the bottom of value reports, separated by a rule.
Use sentence case for column headings, with SKU as the only all-caps heading.
Order report columns from identity to detail: SKU, name, location, quantities, value.
When a listing is empty, say what was searched: `No items match "bolt" at MAIN.`
Follow an empty-state sentence with one next step the user can take.
Never answer an empty result with no text at all in interactive use.
Avoid internal words such as "ledger row" or "backend" in user text; say "movement" and "data file".
Do not show movement UUIDs in default reports; show them only in detailed views.
Show progress for any operation that takes more than two seconds.
Show progress as done and total, for example `Counted 1,240 of 3,000 items`.
Do not draw progress bars when the result goes to a pipe or a file.
End a bulk action with one summary sentence: `Moved 18 items, skipped 2.`
List skipped items with the reason for each after the summary line.
Never use colour as the only signal; low-stock rows also carry a marker such as `!`.
Keep piped results free of banners and decoration so they can feed another tool directly.
Keep the machine-readable mode free of decoration so scripts can depend on it.
Keep vague words like "recently" or "soon" out of exported data; they belong only in interactive views.
Ask a docs reviewer to read any PR that adds or changes user-facing sentences.
Do not blame the user in text: say `This SKU is not known`, not `You entered a wrong SKU`.
When a SKU is not found, suggest the closest known SKU if one is near.
Keep each user-facing sentence to one idea and under 20 words.
Do not put a full stop at the end of headings, column titles or menu entries.
End full sentences in user text with a full stop.
Use US English spelling in user text and docs: "color", "canceled", "license".
Use the serial comma in lists in user text: `SKU, location, and quantity`.
Write movements as quantity, unit, SKU, then place: `40 EA BOLT-M6 to MAIN/A03/B12`.
Use "from" and "to" for moves, never arrows, in user text.
Say "below reorder point", not "low stock", when the reorder rule triggered.
Say "reserved for <holder>" when explaining why stock is not available.
Keep interactive prompts to one line that ends with the expected answer format.
Do not remember answers to prompts between runs; every run asks again.
After a reversible action, tell the user how to reverse it in one short sentence.
Before an irreversible action, say plainly that it cannot be reversed.
Keep successful runs short: one line for a single action, a summary for bulk actions.
A detailed view may add rows but must keep the wording of the lines the short view shows.
Give each report a one-line title that names the scope: `Stock on hand at MAIN`.
Show the filters that shaped a report under its title so a pasted report explains itself.
Mark truncated cells with an ellipsis and never cut a SKU.
Page interactive listings longer than one screen through the user's pager.
Give every public name a page or section in the API reference.
Keep every code example in the docs runnable against the current release.
Treat a wording change in user-facing sentences as a minor change, never as a breaking one.
Read the whole module before you edit it, not only the function you plan to change.
Grep first to find the relevant lines, then read the targeted range instead of the full file.
Do not read the same section of a file twice without a code change in between.
For any change that touches more than two modules, write a short plan before the first edit.
Give each plan step a check you can run, such as `make check` or a single test module.
Collect every open question before you start and ask them together, not one at a time.
If a new ambiguity shows up halfway through, stop and ask instead of picking an answer silently.
State each assumption you made in the final report so a reviewer can reject it quickly.
Touch only the files the request needs; leave nearby cleanup for a separate change.
Mention unrelated bugs you notice in the report, but do not fix them in the same diff.
Do not reformat untouched code; a whitespace-only diff hides the real change from reviewers.
Remove only the code your change made unused; leave older dead code for its own cleanup.
Never say a task is done until the full suite passes locally with `make check`.
In the report, list the exact commands you ran and whether each one passed.
If you could not run a check, say so plainly instead of implying it passed.
Do not skip, delete, or weaken a failing test to make the suite pass.
A skipped test needs a linked issue in the skip reason, for example `skip("see #412")`.
Capture long command output to a file once, then search that file instead of running the command again.
Do not run the same test command again without a code change; read the saved output instead.
Group related edits across files, then run the suite once, not after each small edit.
Never hand-edit generated files; change the source and run `make gen`.
For generated files under `build/` and `dist/`, search only; do not read them in full.
Put scratch scripts and sample data in the session scratch folder, never in the repo tree.
Delete any temporary file you created in the repo before you finish the task.
Check `git status` before you report and remove files you did not mean to add.
Prefer a few small, focused diffs over one large diff that mixes concerns.
Keep each commit to one concern so it can be reverted alone.
For a bug fix, write a test that fails on the current code, then make it pass.
Every bug fix ships with a regression test that would have caught the bug.
Mention the issue number in the regression test body so the next reader can find the report.
Use obviously fake data in fixtures, such as SKU `TEST-0001` and warehouse `WH-FAKE`.
Never copy real supplier names, addresses, or price lists into fixtures.
Use fakes only at the I/O edge; run real domain code everywhere else.
Do not mock the item model or the quantity math; build real objects with small fixtures.
Tests must give the same result on every run; seed any random input with a fixed value.
Tests never reach the network; a test that needs a remote service is out of scope for this repo.
Do not use sleeps to wait in tests; drive the code to the state you need directly.
Test what a caller can see, not private attributes or the order of internal calls.
Prove behaviour through the public package surface, not through underscored modules.
Give each test its own temporary folder for data files so tests never share state on disk.
Do not share a mutable fixture between tests; build a fresh one in each test.
Tests must pass in any order and when run alone.
Cover the zero, one, and many cases for any code that counts or sums quantities.
Add a case for negative quantities wherever stock can be adjusted down.
Keep line coverage at or above the current floor in `make coverage`; do not lower the floor in a feature PR.
New code needs tests for its main path and at least one edge case before review.
Do not add tests that only touch lines for coverage; each test must check a real behaviour.
Keep each test short and about one behaviour; split a test that checks three things.
Lay out each test as setup, one action, then the checks, separated by a blank line.
Do not add hooks or switches to production code only so a test can reach inside.
Give factory builders safe defaults so a test sets only the fields it cares about.
Keep expected report text in golden files under `tests/golden/` and refresh them with `make golden`.
Read every golden file diff before you commit it; never refresh golden files blindly.
Run the focused test module first, then the full suite before you report.
Run `make check` before you push; CI runs the same target and will fail on the same things.
Treat a flaky test as a bug; fix it or open an issue, never rerun until it passes.
Before a refactor, confirm the suite is green, and keep it green after each step.
A refactor commit must not change behaviour; put behaviour changes in a separate commit.
Refactor in small steps that each leave the code working, not in one large rewrite.
Say in the PR title when a change is a pure refactor, for example `refactor: split movement module`.
Do not add an abstraction for a second use case that does not exist yet.
Extract shared code only after the third copy, not the second.
Inline a small function that has only one caller and adds no clarity.
Never reset, stash, or overwrite changes in the working tree that you did not make.
Ask before any command that deletes data files, rewrites history, or force-pushes.
Do not commit or push unless the person asks you to.
Match the style of the surrounding module even where you would write it another way.
Read `CONTRIBUTING.md` once per session before your first change to the repo.
When a package folder has its own README, read it before you edit files in that folder.
If a subfolder has its own agent guide, its rules win over this file for files in that folder.
When you explain a finding, cite the file and line, such as `stock/ledger.py:88`.
Start the final report with a one-to-three sentence summary of the result.
Do not recap every step in the final report; list only what a reviewer needs to act on.
Separate what you checked by running code from what you only read in the source.
Do not guess how a standard library call behaves; read its docs or try it in a scratch script.
Try an unclear behaviour in a short scratch script before you build a change on top of it.
Shrink a bug to the smallest set of items and commands that still shows it before you fix it.
Paste the minimal reproduction into the issue so others can confirm the fix.
Fix the root cause, not the symptom; a guard that hides a wrong count is not a fix.
In the PR, explain why the bug happened in one or two sentences, not only what changed.
Do not add a workaround without a linked issue that tracks the real fix.
Every TODO must carry an issue number, for example `TODO(#231): merge with transfer path`.
Do not leave a TODO you could finish in the same change; finish it instead.
Read only the files you need for the task; do not open the whole package to get oriented.
Start from the module map in this file to find code, and only then search the tree.
Use the `make` targets instead of calling tools directly so you get the pinned versions.
Run `make` with no target to see the list of available tasks before you invent a new one.
Do not add a new developer tool or script without asking first.
Install packages only into the project virtual env, never into the system interpreter.
Never run a global package install to unblock a task; ask instead.
The test suite must run with no network access; check that before you add a test.
Keep fixture files small; five items and a few movements show most behaviours.
Write fixture rows so a reviewer can check them by eye, with round numbers and clear SKUs.
Keep shared fixture data under `tests/fixtures/` and do not copy it into test modules.
Use fixed ids in fixtures so golden files stay the same between runs.
If a test needs random data, seed the generator with a fixed number in the test itself.
Do not rely on dict or set iteration order unless the code under test sorts it.
Use a table of input and expected pairs when one behaviour needs many cases.
Run table cases as subtests so one bad row does not hide the others.
A test should fail for one reason only; split it when two checks are independent.
Compare whole values, such as the full row, so a failed check shows the reader what differed.
For every backend, test that a saved item reads back equal to the one written.
Run the same behaviour cases against every storage backend, not only the default one.
Add a case for an interrupted write wherever a backend writes more than one file.
Add a case with two writers for any code path that changes stock under a lock.
For quantity math, add cases that check sums stay the same after a move between locations.
Add one case with ten thousand items to code that walks the whole inventory.
Include a non-ASCII item name in fixtures for any code that sorts or matches names.
Every report command needs a case with an empty inventory.
Each command needs at least one end-to-end case that runs it through the entry point.
Keep each test under a second; move slower ones to the `slow` suite run by `make check-slow`.
Do not add a third-party package just for tests; the standard library is enough here.
Do a rename in its own commit with no other change, so review is a quick scan.
Move code between modules in its own commit, without edits to the moved lines.
A refactor must not change any public name; if one must change, it is a feature PR with a deprecation.
If an area has no tests, add pinning tests that record current behaviour before you refactor it.
Stop a refactor when the goal is met; do not keep tidying the next module over.
For a refactor done for speed, show the before and after numbers from `make bench` in the PR.
Pull pure calculation out of I/O code so you can test it without files on disk.
Avoid deep chains of pass-through functions; a call that only forwards its inputs can go.
Prefer a flat module layout; add a subpackage only when a folder would hold five or more modules.
Use early returns to keep the main path at the left margin instead of nesting branches.
Split a function that no longer fits on one screen into named steps.
Avoid short abbreviations in names; write `quantity`, not `qty`. SKU is the one accepted short form.
Do not change a list or dict passed in by the caller; build and give back a new one.
Keep quantity math in pure functions that take values and give back values.
Keep each fact in one place; if two modules hold the same number, one of them is wrong soon.
Do not add a second code path that does the same job as an existing one; extend the first.
Before you change a function, find all its callers with grep and read each call site.
When you change a shared module, run the tests of every module that uses it.
Keep a PR under about 400 changed lines; split larger work into a stack of PRs.
Open a draft PR early for large work so a maintainer can comment on the direction.
Read your own diff top to bottom before you ask for review.
Every PR description ends with a short test plan listing the commands you ran.
For a change to command text the user sees, paste the before and after terminal text into the PR.
Do not resolve a review thread someone else opened; let the reviewer resolve it.
Push review fixes as new commits during review; squash only when the reviewer approves.
If CI is red on your PR, fix it before asking for another review round.
Reproduce a CI failure locally with the same make target before you change code for it.
Do not rerun a failed CI job without reading its output first.
Check the known flaky list in `tests/FLAKY.md` before you blame your change for a random failure.
Move a confirmed flaky test to quarantine with an issue link; do not delete it.
If a bug hunt passes an hour with no lead, write down what you tried and ask for a second view.
Keep notes of each hypothesis you tested and its result so the next person does not repeat them.
Ask a short question as soon as you are blocked rather than guessing at a large design.
Say when you are not sure; a confident wrong answer costs more review than an honest maybe.
Back each claim about current behaviour with the file you read or the command you ran.
Before you accept a review claim of a bug, reproduce it with a short case.
Do not add features the request did not ask for, even small ones.
Do not add new user choices to a command unless the request asks for them.
Prefer the simplest change that solves the stated problem.
Before you push, ask yourself whether a senior maintainer would call the change too complex.
If a fix grows past twice the size you expected, step back and look for a smaller one.
Do not copy a block of more than five lines; move it into a shared function instead.
Remove branches that no caller can reach once you have proved it with grep.
After a behaviour change, search the docs for the old behaviour and update every mention.
Run every example in `examples/` after you change the public API.
Keep examples covered by `make examples` so CI catches a broken one.
Do not leave trailing whitespace or a missing final newline in files you touch.
Run `make lint` before review; a reviewer should never point out what a linter can find.
Do not silence a lint rule inline to get green; fix the code or ask to change the rule.
Change lint rules in their own PR, with the fixes the new rule needs.
Let the formatter own layout; do not argue about layout in review.
Pin developer tool versions in `requirements-dev.txt` so every machine gets the same results.
Bump developer tool versions in a separate PR, never inside a feature change.
Before a large PR, run the suite in a fresh clone to catch files you forgot to add.
A green local run means nothing if a needed file is untracked; check `git status` again.
Do not commit paths from your own machine, such as a home folder, in code or fixtures.
Keep personal notes out of the repo; use the session scratch folder for them.
Make sure `.claude/worktrees/` is in `.gitignore` before you add a worktree.
When work is split across agents, give each one a separate set of files to avoid edit clashes.
When you hand work to another agent, list the files changed, checks run, and open questions.
Do not push new features to a PR that is under review; open a follow-up instead.
File an issue for each follow-up you defer, and link it in the PR.
After merge, run the reproduction once on `main` to confirm the fix landed.
After you write a new test, break the code on purpose once to see the test fail.
Do not leave tests commented out; skip them with a reason or delete them.
Never pass state between tests through module globals.
Remove any file a test writes, even when the test fails partway.
Tests never write to the home folder or the current folder; use a temporary one.
Give fixture items fixed ids so ordering in reports stays the same between runs.
Sort report rows by SKU in tests so differences point at real changes.
If a test needs more than three fixtures, the code under test probably does too much.
Test a command by calling the package entry point, not by calling its inner functions.
Use the in-memory backend as the fake for command tests; keep file backends for their own cases.
Do not close a bug issue until a regression test for it has merged.
Look at the coverage report for your diff and add tests for any new lines it marks as missed.
Add a case at exactly the reorder point for any code that decides when stock is low.
Cover a move that asks for more units than the source location holds.
If the request and the docs both say nothing about a case, ask; do not invent the rule.
Revert any experimental edit that did not make it into the final change before you report.
Sort the reorder report by shortfall, largest first, so buyers see the most urgent SKUs at the top.
Never convert between units of measure without a conversion row for that item; refuse the move instead.
Keep one concern per pull request: a bug fix, a feature or a refactor, never two of them.
Ask a second reviewer for any change that alters how on-hand quantity is derived from the movement ledger.
Keep example data sets in the docs under twenty items so a reader can follow every row.
Write one purchase draft per supplier; never mix lines for two suppliers in one draft.
Sort count sheets by bin path so a counter can walk the aisle in order.
The `stock` package never opens a network connection; all data stays on the local disk.
Treat stock in the quarantine bin as on hand but not available; reports show both numbers.
Merge only after every required check is green on the latest push, not on an earlier one.
Block any movement that would take on-hand quantity below zero at a location in strict mode.
Record a transfer as two movements, an issue at the source and a receipt at the target, sharing one transfer id.
While a count is open for a bin, refuse new movements into or out of that bin.
Every manual adjustment carries a reason code from the fixed list: damaged, lost, found, recount.
A reservation can never exceed available quantity; partial reservations are not allowed.
Compare SKUs without regard to case, but keep the case the user first entered for display.
Bin path segments are short codes such as `MAIN/R2/04`; do not put free text in a bin path.
End every quantity report with a totals row, and make sure the totals match the sum of the rows above.
The valuation method is weighted average cost; do not add FIFO or LIFO without a design discussion.
Reviewers check that a data migration has a matching downgrade note in the PR, even if no downgrade code ships.
Ask reporters for the item and movement counts of their data set; most slowness reports depend on size.
Keep the table of supported units of measure in the user guide in sync with the units the code accepts.
When a change alters a report, attach the report for the sample data set before and after the change.
Reservations always belong to a named order reference; never create an anonymous hold.
Archive a supplier that is no longer used; do not delete it while movements still refer to it.
Reorder points are set per item and warehouse, not globally per item.
Change one model per PR when you can; model changes ripple through storage, reports and docs.
When a request could be read two ways, ask the maintainer which one they mean before you write code.
Use fictional supplier and item names in sample data; never copy names from a real company.

prose.heading: Storage layer overview
prose.text:
The storage layer is the only part of `stock` that touches disk. Everything above it, the models and the commands, speaks in terms of items, locations and movements, and never knows whether the data lives in a SQLite file, a directory of flat files, or a dictionary in memory. A backend gets a small surface: read the item table, append movements, read movements in order, and commit a batch. Nothing else is part of the contract.

This split is load-bearing. When a command needs something the surface does not give, the answer is almost never a new backend method. First check whether the model layer can derive it from movements it already reads. Add a method to the backend surface only when every backend can implement it with the same meaning, and add it to all of them in the same pull request.

prose.heading: The three backends
prose.text:
There are three backends today. The SQLite backend is the default for real use and the one most users run. The flat-file backend keeps one item table and one movement file per warehouse in a plain directory, so that people can keep their stock under version control and read diffs by eye. The memory backend exists for tests and for the interactive demo; it keeps nothing after the process ends.

All three pass the same contract suite in `tests/contract/`. If you change how a backend behaves, run that suite against all three, not only the one you touched. A behaviour that only one backend shows is a bug in that backend, even when the behaviour looks better.

prose.heading: The movement ledger
prose.text:
`stock` does not keep a quantity column. Every change to inventory is a movement: a signed quantity of one item, at one location, with a reason code and a sequence number. On-hand quantity is the sum of movements for that item and location. A receipt adds, a pick subtracts, a transfer is two movements that share a transfer id, and a count adjustment is whatever difference the count found.

The ledger is append-only. A wrong movement is never edited or deleted; it is reversed by a new movement with the opposite sign and the reason `reversal`, which points back at the original. This keeps the history honest and lets `stock report history` show exactly what happened and in which order. Code that tries to update a movement in place will not pass review.

prose.heading: How on-hand is computed
prose.text:
Summing the whole ledger on every read would be slow for a warehouse with years of history, so the model layer keeps a snapshot. A snapshot records the on-hand total per item and location up to a given sequence number. To answer "how many of SKU A-100 are in bin R2-04", the model reads the latest snapshot and adds the movements after it.

Snapshots are a cache, not a source of truth. They can be deleted at any time and `stock rebuild` will recompute them from the ledger. If a snapshot and the ledger ever disagree, the ledger wins, and the disagreement is a bug to report with the sequence numbers involved. Never write a fix that patches a snapshot to match a number you expect.

prose.heading: Reservations
prose.text:
A reservation holds a quantity of an item for an order without moving it. Reservations live beside the ledger, not in it, because they are intent rather than fact: nothing has left the shelf yet. Available quantity is on-hand minus open reservations at the same location.

A reservation is open, fulfilled or released. Fulfilling one writes the pick movement and closes the reservation in the same commit, so there is no moment where both the reservation and the pick count against the shelf. Releasing one writes nothing to the ledger. When you add a command that moves stock, ask whether it must look at reservations; most do, and the ones that forget them are the most common source of over-picking reports.

prose.heading: Locations and bins
prose.text:
A location is a path: warehouse, then zone, then bin, written `MAIN/R2/04`. Only bins hold stock. Warehouses and zones are groupings for reports and for permissions in the shared deployment. A movement against a zone or warehouse path is rejected by the model layer before it reaches storage.

Paths are case-insensitive for lookup but keep the case the user first typed for display. Renaming a bin is a ledger-neutral operation: it changes the path in the location table and leaves every movement pointing at the same location id. Deleting a bin is only allowed when its on-hand is zero for every item and it has no open reservations.

prose.heading: Units of measure
prose.text:
Every item has a base unit, such as `each`, `kg` or `m`. Movements are always stored in the base unit. Packaging units, like a case of 12 or a pallet of 40 cases, are conversions defined on the item, and the CLI converts at the edge: a user may receive `3 case` and the ledger records 36 `each`.

Conversions are exact integer or decimal factors. We do not store floats anywhere in the ledger, because a weight of 0.1 kg added ten times must equal exactly 1 kg. Items sold by weight or length use `Decimal` with a fixed scale set on the item. Changing an item's base unit after it has movements is not supported; create a new item and transfer the stock instead.

prose.heading: Reorder points
prose.text:
Each item may carry a reorder point and a reorder quantity per warehouse. `stock report reorder` lists every item whose available quantity, not on-hand quantity, is at or below its reorder point. Using available quantity means open reservations pull an item toward reorder sooner, which is what buyers asked for.

The report does not place orders. It produces a list that a person reviews, and the optional supplier export turns that list into a purchase draft per supplier. Keep it that way: an earlier prototype that wrote purchase orders on its own created duplicates every time two people ran the report on the same morning.

prose.heading: Counts and reconciliation
prose.text:
A cycle count is a session. It starts with `stock count start` for a set of bins, takes entered quantities, and ends with `stock count close`. While a session is open, movements to its bins are still allowed, and the session remembers the sequence number at which each bin was counted.

On close, the model compares each counted quantity with the on-hand at that bin's sequence number, not with the current on-hand. The difference becomes one adjustment movement per item and bin, with the reason `count` and the session id. This is why a pick in the middle of a count does not show up as shrinkage. If you change the close step, keep the per-bin sequence number; it is the whole point of the design.

prose.heading: Data format versions
prose.text:
Every data directory and every SQLite file carries a format version, a single integer. The current version is 7. On start, `stock` reads the version and refuses to work on data from a newer version than it knows. Data from an older version must be migrated with `stock migrate` before other commands will run against it.

A migration is a function from version N to N+1 in `stock/migrations/`. Migrations run in order and each one commits on its own, so an interrupted run can be resumed from where it stopped. Do not edit a migration that has shipped in a release. If a shipped migration was wrong, add a new one that repairs the data.

prose.heading: Writing a migration
prose.text:
A good migration does one thing. Adding a column and backfilling it from the ledger are two migrations, not one, because a backfill can be slow and a user who interrupts it should still have a usable schema. Every migration needs a fixture of real-looking data at the old version and a check that the new version reads it the same way.

Migrations must be the same for every backend at the level of meaning, even when the code differs. The flat-file backend migrates by rewriting files into a temporary directory and swapping it in; the SQLite backend uses a transaction. In both cases the user either sees the old version or the new one, never a half-migrated mix.

prose.heading: Locking and concurrent writers
prose.text:
Several people may point `stock` at the same data, most often a shared SQLite file on a network drive or a flat-file directory in a synced folder. Writers take an exclusive lock for the length of one commit. Readers do not lock; they read a consistent view because movements are appended and snapshots are swapped in whole.

The lock is a lock file next to the data with the holder's host name and process id inside. A stale lock from a crashed process is detected by checking whether that process still exists on the same host. Locks from another host are never broken automatically; `stock unlock` exists for that, and it asks the user to confirm. Please do not add a timeout that breaks remote locks. We tried it in 2022 and it caused two lost commits in one week.

prose.heading: Crash safety
prose.text:
A commit must survive a power cut at any instant. For SQLite this is the database's own job, and we keep the journal mode at WAL and never turn off synchronous writes. For the flat-file backend, a commit writes the new movement lines to a temporary file, flushes and syncs it, then appends it to the movement file with a single rename-and-concatenate step guarded by the lock.

When you touch commit code, think about what a reader sees if the process dies between any two lines. If the answer is "a partial movement", the change is wrong. The crash suite in `tests/crash/` kills a child process at random points during a commit and checks that the data reads back cleanly. Run it locally before you ask for review on anything in the commit path.

prose.heading: Decision: SQLite as the default backend
prose.text:
In 2021 the default backend was the flat-file one. It was easy to inspect and easy to sync, and for a shop with a few hundred items it was fast enough. In early 2023 we made SQLite the default because three of our larger users had warehouses with more than two million movements, and reading the movement files took several seconds per command.

The flat-file backend stays fully supported. Its readers are a real group, mostly small shops and people who like to see their stock in git. What changed is only what a new user gets when they run `stock init` with no other choice. Do not describe the flat-file backend as legacy in the docs or in review comments.

prose.heading: Decision: append-only ledger
prose.text:
The first version of `stock` kept a quantity per item and bin and updated it in place. Every bug report about a wrong quantity ended the same way: nobody could tell how the number got there. In 2020 we moved to the append-only ledger described above and made on-hand a derived value.

The cost is disk space and a snapshot cache to keep reads fast. The gain is that every number can be explained, every mistake can be reversed without losing the record of it, and audits are a query instead of an investigation. When a proposal would bring back in-place updates for speed, the answer is to improve snapshots, not to give up the ledger.

prose.heading: Decision: Decimal quantities
prose.text:
Until version 0.9, quantities were floats. A bakery using `stock` for flour reported that their flour totals in kg drifted by a few grams per month, and that a count adjustment of zero kept appearing after every count. Both came from float rounding. In 0.10 we moved every quantity to `Decimal` with a scale fixed per item.

The scale is part of the item, not of the movement, so two movements of the same item always add exactly. The migration that made this change is version 4, and it rounds old float values to the item's scale. That rounding was reviewed with the bakery and two other users before release; it is not something to repeat casually.

prose.heading: Decision: no ORM
prose.text:
`stock` talks to SQLite with plain SQL in one module per table. We looked at an ORM in 2022 and chose not to adopt one. The package has no runtime dependencies outside the standard library, and that is a promise to users who install it on locked-down warehouse machines. An ORM would also hide the exact statements, and for a tool where commit order matters, we want the statements in plain view.

The cost is some repetition in the SQL modules. Accept it. A small shared module builds placeholders and row mappings, and that is as far as abstraction should go. If you find yourself writing a query builder, stop and ask on the issue first.

prose.heading: Decision: flat-file layout
prose.text:
The flat-file backend stores the item table as a tab-separated file and movements as one line per movement in a separate file per warehouse. We chose tab-separated text in 2019 because users wanted to open their data in a spreadsheet, and because line-per-movement files diff cleanly in git.

Each movement line carries the sequence number first, so `sort -n` puts lines back in order if a sync tool ever reorders lines. Fields never contain tabs or newlines; the model layer rejects such values on input. When you add a field, add it at the end of the line and bump the format version. Older readers ignore trailing fields they do not know only within the same major format, so a new field always needs a migration.

prose.heading: Decision: transfers as movement pairs
prose.text:
A transfer between two bins could have been one record with a source and a target. We chose two movements, a negative one at the source and a positive one at the target, joined by a transfer id. The reason is that every report and every snapshot only has to understand one shape of record: a signed quantity at one place.

The two movements are always written in the same commit. A transfer that crosses warehouses still uses the same pair, and the in-transit state, when a user enables it, is a third location named `TRANSIT` inside the receiving warehouse. Code that reads transfers must never assume the pair is adjacent in the ledger; other movements can sit between them in sequence order.

prose.heading: Decision: one package, no plugins
prose.text:
In 2022 a contributor proposed a plugin system so that other people could ship their own backends. We declined. Every backend must pass the contract suite and the crash suite, and must keep the same meaning for every movement. A plugin loaded from somewhere else would carry none of those promises, and the bug reports would still come to us.

New backends are welcome as pull requests to this repository, with the full suites passing. A backend that cannot pass them, for example one that cannot commit a transfer pair atomically, is not a backend for `stock`. That rule has turned away two proposals so far, a spreadsheet API and a key-value cloud service, and both proposers agreed after seeing the crash suite fail.

prose.heading: Decision: standard library only
prose.text:
`stock` has no runtime dependencies. The promise dates from version 0.3, when a user in a pharmacy chain told us their machines could only install packages that passed a security review, and each dependency took weeks to approve. A single wheel with nothing else to pull was the reason they could adopt the tool at all.

Development dependencies are a different matter and are listed in `requirements-dev.txt`. They never ship. When a feature would be much easier with a third-party package, write the small piece of it you need, or leave the feature out. Pull requests that add an install requirement are closed with a link to this section.

prose.heading: Pitfall: transfers and reservations
prose.text:
A transfer moves on-hand, but it does not move reservations. If an order reserved ten units in bin A and someone transfers all of bin A to bin B, the reservation still points at bin A, where available quantity is now negative. The model layer blocks this case: a transfer may only move the unreserved part of a bin unless the user also moves the reservations.

New commands that move stock between bins must go through the same transfer path in the model layer to get this check. We have had two regressions from code that wrote the movement pair directly through the backend. If you need a variant of transfer, extend the model function rather than writing a second one.

prose.heading: Pitfall: negative on-hand
prose.text:
On-hand can go negative, and this is on purpose. In a real warehouse, a picker often ships an item before the receipt is entered. If `stock` refused the pick, the user would invent a fake receipt to get past it, and the ledger would lie.

So a pick that takes a bin below zero is allowed, and the bin shows up in `stock report negative` until a receipt or count brings it back. Do not add a guard that blocks negative on-hand in the model layer, and do not hide negative bins in reports. A shop that wants stricter rules can turn on strict mode per warehouse, and that mode lives in one place only.

prose.heading: Pitfall: unit conversions at the edge
prose.text:
Conversion between packaging units and the base unit happens once, at the edge, when user input is parsed. Below that line, every quantity is in the base unit. Bugs appear when code deep in the model layer tries to convert again because it sees a number that looks too large.

If a quantity looks wrong in the model layer, find where it entered. Do not add a second conversion "just in case". Reports show packaging units only when the user asks for them, and that conversion is again done at the edge, on the way out. A quick check: if a function below the CLI layer takes a unit name as a parameter, it is probably in the wrong layer.

prose.heading: Pitfall: stale snapshots after manual edits
prose.text:
Users of the flat-file backend sometimes edit movement files by hand, most often to fix a typo in a reference field. That is allowed, but the snapshot cache does not know about it. A snapshot built before the edit stays valid by sequence number while the data under it changed.

`stock` checks a digest of each movement file against the one recorded with the snapshot and drops the snapshot when they differ. This check costs a full read of the file and is the main reason the flat-file backend is slower to start. Do not remove it to gain speed. If start time matters, the right work is to make the digest incremental, which is an open issue.

prose.heading: Pitfall: bin renames in reports
prose.text:
Because movements point at a location id, a renamed bin shows its new path for its whole history. This surprises people who pull up a report from last year and see a bin name that did not exist then. It is correct behaviour for stock purposes, and the history report adds a note when a path was renamed after the period.

When you write a new report, reuse the shared path display function so that the rename note appears consistently. Do not join on the path text anywhere, in reports or in migrations. Two bins can have had the same path at different times, and the id is the only stable key.

prose.heading: Pitfall: data on shared drives
prose.text:
SQLite on a network drive is risky. File locking over SMB and NFS is not always honest, and two writers on different machines can each believe they hold the lock. We document this in the README and recommend the flat-file backend in a synced folder, or a single machine that others reach over remote desktop.

When a user reports a corrupted SQLite file, ask first where the file lives. Most of these reports come from shared drives. Do not try to make `stock` safe on every network file system; it is not a problem a small tool can solve, and partial fixes give people false confidence.

prose.heading: Glossary: items and quantities
prose.text:
**Item**: a thing that is counted, identified by its SKU. Each item has a base unit and a quantity scale.

**SKU**: the stock-keeping unit code, unique per data set and case-insensitive. Users choose the format; `stock` only checks that it is non-empty and has no whitespace.

**On-hand**: the quantity physically present at a location, derived by summing movements.

**Available**: on-hand minus open reservations at the same location. This is the number pick lists and reorder reports use.

**Base unit**: the unit the ledger stores. Packaging units convert to it with an exact factor.

prose.heading: Glossary: ledger terms
prose.text:
**Movement**: one signed change in quantity of one item at one location, with a reason code and a sequence number.

**Reason code**: why a movement happened. The fixed set is `receipt`, `pick`, `transfer`, `count`, `reversal`, `scrap` and `return`. New codes need a migration because reports group by them.

**Sequence number**: the order in which the backend committed a movement. It is the only order code may rely on.

**Reversal**: a movement that cancels an earlier one by writing the opposite quantity and pointing back to it.

**Snapshot**: a cached on-hand total per item and location up to a sequence number. Snapshots can be thrown away and rebuilt.

prose.heading: Glossary: places
prose.text:
**Warehouse**: the top level of a location path. Permissions in shared setups and the reorder report work per warehouse.

**Zone**: a grouping of bins inside a warehouse, for reports only. Zones never hold stock directly.

**Bin**: the leaf of a location path and the only place stock can sit.

**Location path**: the slash-separated name of a bin, such as `MAIN/R2/04`. Lookup ignores case; display keeps it.

**Transit**: an optional bin named `TRANSIT` in the receiving warehouse, which holds stock that has left one warehouse and not yet arrived at another.

prose.heading: Glossary: orders and counts
prose.text:
**Reservation**: a hold on available quantity for an order, without a movement. It is open, fulfilled or released.

**Fulfil**: close a reservation by writing the pick movement in the same commit.

**Count session**: a set of bins counted together, from `stock count start` to `stock count close`.

**Counted-at sequence**: the sequence number at which a bin was counted inside a session. The close step compares against on-hand at that number.

**Adjustment**: the movement a count close writes for each difference it finds, with reason `count`.

**Shrinkage**: the total negative adjustment from counts over a period, reported per warehouse.

prose.heading: Glossary: purchasing
prose.text:
**Reorder point**: the available quantity at or below which an item should be ordered again, set per item and warehouse.

**Reorder quantity**: how much to order when an item hits its reorder point. It is a suggestion; the buyer decides.

**Supplier**: a party that sells an item. One item may have several suppliers with a preferred one.

**Lead time**: the number of days a supplier usually takes to deliver. The reorder report shows it but does not use it to change the reorder point.

**Purchase draft**: the per-supplier list the reorder export produces for a person to review and send.

prose.heading: Glossary: data and storage
prose.text:
**Data set**: everything one `stock` installation reads and writes: items, locations, movements, reservations, snapshots and the format version.

**Backend**: the code that keeps a data set on disk or in memory. There are three: SQLite, flat-file and memory.

**Format version**: the integer that says which layout a data set uses. The current one is 7.

**Migration**: a step that moves a data set from one format version to the next.

**Contract suite**: the shared checks every backend must pass, in `tests/contract/`.

**Crash suite**: checks that kill a writer at random points and verify the data still reads cleanly.

prose.heading: Project history: the first years
prose.text:
`stock` started in 2018 as a single script that a hardware shop used to track screws and fittings across two storerooms. The first public release, 0.1, came a year later with the flat-file backend and four commands: add, take, move and list.

The 0.x series grew the model we have today. Version 0.4 brought locations as paths, 0.6 the reservation model, 0.8 cycle counts, and 0.10 decimal quantities. The append-only ledger came in 0.5 and was the largest single change in the project's life; it required every user to run the first migration we ever shipped. We still keep that migration in the tree, and the oldest fixture in `tests/fixtures/v1/` comes from the hardware shop's real data, scrubbed of prices.

prose.heading: Project history: 1.0 and after
prose.text:
Version 1.0 shipped in 2023 with SQLite as the default backend, the snapshot cache, and a promise of a stable library surface for the model layer. Since then, minor releases have added features without breaking that surface, and every format change has come with a migration.

The 1.x line also brought the contract suite, which started as a set of checks copied between backend test modules and became shared when the third backend arrived. Planned for 2.0 are a cleaner reservation surface and the removal of two deprecated report shapes. Nothing in 2.0 will change the ledger model. If you see a proposal labelled `2.0` that does, it needs a design discussion first.

prose.heading: Layers of the package
prose.text:
The package has three layers. `stock/models/` holds the domain: items, locations, movements, reservations, counts, and the functions that check and combine them. `stock/storage/` holds the backends and the contract they share. `stock/commands/` holds the CLI: it parses what the user typed, calls the model layer, and formats what comes back.

Dependencies point one way only. Commands may use models and storage; models may use the storage contract but no backend in particular; storage knows nothing about either. A model module that reaches for a specific backend, or a backend that calls a model function, breaks the layering, and review will ask you to move the code. The layer test in `tests/layers/` reads the source tree and fails on such a reference.

prose.heading: The library surface
prose.text:
Some users call `stock` from their own Python code instead of the CLI, most often to feed a web shop or a label maker. For them, the model layer is a public library. Its stable surface is what `stock.models` exposes at the package level and what the reference page in `docs/library.md` lists.

Changes to that surface follow the deprecation policy: a renamed function keeps the old name as an alias for at least one minor release, with a deprecation notice, and is removed only in the next major release. Internal modules under `stock/models/_internal/` carry no promise. If a user depends on one of them, the answer is to expose a supported function, not to freeze the internal one.

prose.heading: How a command runs
prose.text:
Every command follows the same path. The entry point reads the user's input and opens the data set through the backend the data set declares. The command then calls one or more model functions, collects the movements and reservation changes they return, and commits them in one batch. Only after the commit succeeds does it format a reply for the user.

Model functions never commit on their own. They return what should be written, and the command decides when. This lets a command that combines several model steps, such as receiving against a purchase draft and fulfilling waiting reservations, put all of it in one commit. If you write a model function that writes to storage directly, the review will ask you to return the changes instead.

prose.heading: How reports are built
prose.text:
A report is a function from a data set and a set of filters to a table of rows. Reports never write. They read snapshots and movements through the model layer, never through a backend directly, so that every report sees on-hand computed the same way.

The CLI then renders the table as aligned text for the terminal or as CSV when the user asks for a file. Rendering is shared by all reports; a report only says which columns it has and how to sort them. When you add a report, add a fixture data set and the expected table for it under `tests/reports/`, and keep the column names in the same words the docs use.

prose.heading: The contract suite
prose.text:
The contract suite in `tests/contract/` is a set of checks written once against the backend surface and run against every backend. It covers ordering of sequence numbers, atomic commits of several movements, reading back exactly what was written including decimal scale, and behaviour when the data set is empty.

A new backend starts by passing this suite and nothing else. A new behaviour in the backend surface starts by adding a check here that every backend fails, then making them all pass. The suite is also the best place to read if you want to know what a backend must do; it is shorter than any of the backends and it is kept accurate because CI runs it.

prose.heading: The memory backend
prose.text:
The memory backend keeps a data set in Python lists and dictionaries for the life of one process. It exists for two reasons: fast tests of the model layer, and `stock demo`, which loads a sample shop so that new users can try commands without creating files.

It still passes the contract suite, including atomic commits, so that model tests run against it mean something. It does not take part in the crash suite, because there is nothing on disk to survive a crash. Do not add features to it that the other backends lack, such as rollback to a past sequence number. Tests that pass only because of such a feature would hide bugs in the real backends.

prose.heading: Item lifecycle
prose.text:
An item is active, archived or merged. Active items take movements. Archived items keep their history but reject new movements, and they drop out of default reports. An item can only be archived when its on-hand is zero everywhere and it has no open reservations.

Merging covers the common case of a duplicate SKU, for example `A-100` and `A100` that turn out to be the same thing. A merge transfers all on-hand from the source item to the target item with movements that carry the reason `transfer` and a merge id, then marks the source item as merged and pointing to the target. The source keeps its history so that old reports still make sense. A merge is never undone by editing; it is undone by a reverse merge.

prose.heading: Lots and serial numbers
prose.text:
Items may be tracked by lot, by serial number, or not at all. A lot-tracked item records a lot code on every movement, and on-hand is kept per item, location and lot. A serial-tracked item is a lot-tracked item where every lot has a quantity of exactly one in the base unit.

Tracking mode is chosen when an item is created and cannot change once the item has movements. Reports group by lot only when asked, so that users who do not care about lots see the same totals as before. When you add a command that moves stock, check whether it must ask for a lot code; the model layer will reject a movement of a lot-tracked item without one.

prose.heading: Returns and scrap
prose.text:
A customer return is a positive movement with the reason `return`, usually into a quarantine bin chosen per warehouse. From quarantine, a person either transfers the goods back to a normal bin or scraps them. Scrap is a negative movement with the reason `scrap` and a short free-text note.

Returns and scrap are kept apart from receipts and count adjustments on purpose. Buyers look at receipts, the finance team looks at scrap, and the warehouse lead looks at count adjustments. Mixing them under one reason would make each of those reports wrong. When a new kind of stock change comes up, ask first whether it is one of these seven reasons in disguise before you propose an eighth.

prose.heading: Strict mode
prose.text:
Strict mode is a per-warehouse choice for shops that want `stock` to refuse picks that would take a bin below zero, and to refuse transfers out of quarantine without a recorded inspection. It is off by default, for the reasons in the negative on-hand section.

All strict checks live in one module, `stock/models/strict.py`, and every command that moves stock calls it through the same gate in the model layer. Do not scatter strict checks into individual commands. A strict check that lives in one command only will be missing from the next command that moves stock, and that is exactly the kind of gap a shop that chose strict mode cannot accept.

prose.heading: Kits
prose.text:
A kit is an item made of other items, such as a first-aid box that holds bandages, tape and gloves. `stock` does not keep on-hand for kits that are assembled on demand; their available quantity is computed from their parts. Kits that are assembled ahead of time are normal items, and assembling them writes a positive movement for the kit and negative movements for each part in one commit.

Kits may not contain other kits more than two levels deep. We set that limit after a customer built a cycle by accident and the availability report never finished. The model layer checks depth and cycles when a kit is saved, not when it is read, so reads stay fast.

prose.heading: Working across warehouses
prose.text:
Most data sets have one warehouse, but the model handles many. Each warehouse has its own reorder points, strict mode choice, quarantine bin and optional transit bin. Items and SKUs are shared across all warehouses in a data set.

Cross-warehouse transfers are the only movements that touch two warehouses, and with transit enabled they become two steps: ship, which moves stock into the receiving warehouse's transit bin, and receive, which moves it from transit to a normal bin. Reports that total across warehouses must state whether they include transit. The default is to include it, because the stock still belongs to the business while it is on a truck.

prose.heading: Backups and copies
prose.text:
`stock backup` writes a copy of a data set to a single archive file. For SQLite it uses the database's own online backup call, so it is safe while others write. For the flat-file backend it takes the write lock, copies the directory, and releases the lock. The archive carries the format version, and `stock unpack` refuses an archive from a newer version.

Users often copy data sets by hand instead, and that is fine when nobody writes during the copy. The docs say so plainly. Do not add a background backup schedule to `stock` itself; the tool runs as a command, not a service, and scheduling belongs to the user's own system.

prose.heading: Exports
prose.text:
Every report can write CSV, and `stock export` writes the full item table, location table and movement ledger as three CSV files. The export is for people, spreadsheets and other systems, not for moving data between `stock` installations; for that, use backups.

The column order in exports is part of the public surface, because users build spreadsheets and scripts on it. New columns go at the end. Removing or renaming a column follows the same deprecation policy as the library surface. Decimal quantities are written at the item's scale with a dot as the separator, whatever the user's locale, so that exports read the same on every machine.

prose.heading: Performance notes
prose.text:
The common commands must answer within a second on a data set of one million movements on an ordinary laptop. The benchmark in `bench/` builds such a data set and times `stock show`, `stock take` and `stock report onhand`. A pull request that slows any of them by more than ten percent needs a reason in its description.

Most time goes to reading movements after the latest snapshot, so snapshot cadence matters. By default a new snapshot is written after every ten thousand movements. Lowering that number speeds reads and slows commits a little. Do not tune it per command; it is a property of the data set, and the trade-off is documented for users in `docs/performance.md`.

prose.heading: Rebuilding snapshots
prose.text:
`stock rebuild` drops every snapshot and computes new ones from the ledger. It is safe at any time and takes the write lock for its whole run, so other writers wait. On a large data set it can take minutes, and it reports progress per warehouse.

Users should rarely need it. The usual reasons are a hand edit in a flat-file data set, an upgrade that changed how snapshots are laid out, or a bug report where we want to rule out a bad cache. When you ask a user to run it while triaging, also ask them for the on-hand numbers before and after; a difference means the snapshot was wrong, and that is a bug worth a fixture.

prose.heading: Decision: no server mode
prose.text:
Users have asked for `stock` to run as a small web server so that several people can share one data set without a network drive. We have said no, for now, three times. A server needs authentication, a network protocol, and a way to run in the background, and each of those is a large surface with its own security work. None of them fit a stdlib-only command-line tool.

The supported way to share is a single machine with the data set and remote access to it, or the flat-file backend in a synced folder with the cautions in the locking section. The library surface makes it easy for someone to build a server on top of `stock` in their own project, and two users have done so.

prose.heading: Decision: case-insensitive SKUs
prose.text:
SKUs are case-insensitive. `a-100` and `A-100` are the same item, and the item table keeps the case first entered. We chose this in 0.2 after a shop ended up with three items for the same part because scanners, people and a supplier sheet all used different case.

The comparison uses `str.casefold`, not `lower`, so that SKUs with letters outside ASCII behave as users expect. The SQLite backend keeps a casefolded copy in an indexed column for lookup; the flat-file backend builds the same index in memory on read. A change to how SKUs compare is a format change, needs a migration, and must handle the case where two existing SKUs collide after the new rule.

prose.heading: Pitfall: changing an item's scale
prose.text:
An item's decimal scale can be increased, for example from two places to three, because every existing movement still fits. It cannot be lowered once the item has movements, because that would mean rounding history.

Increasing the scale is a migration of one item's data, and the command runs it in one commit with the item change. Code that reads movements must not assume the scale on a movement equals the item's current scale; old movements may have fewer places. Always quantize to the current item scale when adding values for display, and never when writing. Mixing those two up has caused off-by-a-cent reports twice.

prose.heading: Pitfall: count sessions left open
prose.text:
A count session that is never closed holds no lock and blocks nothing, which is by design. But an open session from weeks ago can confuse people, because `stock count close` will compare against on-hand at the old counted-at sequence numbers and write adjustments for movements that happened long before.

`stock count list` shows open sessions with their age, and `stock count abandon` closes a session without writing adjustments. The close step warns when a session is more than seven days old and asks the user to confirm. Do not change close to recount automatically; a recount is a new physical count, and only a person can do it.

prose.heading: Pitfall: memory backend in tests
prose.text:
Model tests run against the memory backend because it is fast. That is fine for checking domain rules, but it hides anything that depends on disk: commit ordering under a lock, reading back decimal scale from text, case of SKUs in the flat-file index. Bugs of that kind pass every model test and fail in real use.

So the rule is simple: a change to how data is written or read needs a check in the contract suite, which runs on every backend. A change to domain rules alone can rely on model tests. If you are not sure which kind your change is, add the contract check; it costs a few seconds of CI.

prose.heading: History of reason codes
prose.text:
The first ledger had three reasons: in, out and fix. In 0.6 they became receipt, pick and count, and transfer was added. Reversal came in 0.7, after users asked how to undo a mistake without deleting it. Scrap and return arrived together in 1.2, at the request of a client that needed shrinkage reports separate from customer returns.

Every addition came with a migration that mapped older records onto the new set, and the old names are still accepted on input as aliases. Reports always show the current names. If you find code that compares a reason to `in` or `out`, it is a leftover from before 0.6, and it should go through the alias map instead.

prose.heading: Glossary: tracking and kits
prose.text:
**Lot**: a batch of an item that shares a lot code, such as a production run. Lot-tracked items keep on-hand per lot.

**Serial**: a lot of exactly one unit. Serial-tracked items are lot-tracked items with that rule.

**Tracking mode**: none, lot or serial. Chosen at item creation and fixed once the item has movements.

**Kit**: an item made of other items. Kits are either assembled ahead of time, as normal items, or computed on demand from their parts.

**Assembly**: the commit that turns parts into an assembled kit: one positive movement for the kit and one negative movement per part.

prose.heading: Glossary: states and modes
prose.text:
**Quarantine bin**: the bin per warehouse where returns land before inspection.

**Strict mode**: a per-warehouse choice that refuses negative on-hand and uninspected quarantine transfers.

**Archived item**: an item with history that takes no new movements and is hidden from default reports.

**Merged item**: a duplicate item whose stock was moved to another item; it keeps its history and points to the target.

**Abandoned session**: a count session closed without writing adjustments.

**Business day**: the day a movement belongs to for reporting, entered by the user and separate from sequence order.

prose.heading: Glossary: project terms
prose.text:
**Contract check**: one check in the contract suite. Every backend must pass all of them.

**Fixture data set**: a small, real-looking data set kept under `tests/fixtures/`, one per format version, used by migration and report checks.

**Layer test**: the check that reads the source tree and refuses references that go against the direction of the layers.

**Bench data set**: the one-million-movement data set that the benchmark builds before timing commands.

**Model function**: a function in the model layer that checks input and returns the changes to commit, without committing them.

prose.heading: Pitfall: forgetting transit
prose.text:
When transit is enabled for a warehouse, stock that has shipped from another warehouse sits in the `TRANSIT` bin until someone receives it. Reports that look only at normal bins will show the stock as missing, and users then enter a count adjustment that later turns into a surplus when the goods are received.

The reorder report counts transit stock as available by default, for this reason. New reports should do the same unless the report is about physical presence on shelves, and then the report title must say so. When triaging a "stock disappeared" issue in a multi-warehouse data set, check the transit bin first.

prose.heading: Release process overview
prose.text:
A release of `stock` is a small, repeatable sequence that any maintainer can run from a clean checkout of `main`. We cut releases when there is something worth shipping, not on a fixed calendar, but we try not to let more than six weeks pass between them so that fixes reach users without a long wait.

Every release goes through the same four stages: freeze, candidate, verification, and publication. Each stage has an owner, and the owner writes a short note in the release tracking issue when the stage is complete. Nobody skips a stage, even for a one-line patch release. If a stage cannot complete, the release stops and the tracking issue says why.

prose.heading: Release step 1: freeze
prose.text:
The freeze starts when the release owner opens a tracking issue titled with the target version and posts it in the maintainers channel. From that moment, only fixes for regressions found during the release may merge into `main`. Feature work continues on branches and waits.

During the freeze the owner reviews every merged pull request since the previous version and sorts it into one of three buckets: user-visible behaviour, internal cleanup, or packaging. That list becomes the summary in the tracking issue and later the text of the GitHub release page. A pull request that nobody can place in a bucket is a sign that its description was too thin; ask the author to expand it before the freeze ends.

prose.heading: Release step 2: candidate
prose.text:
The candidate is built from the head of `main` at the freeze by the release workflow, never from a local machine. The workflow builds the wheel and the source distribution, runs the full suite against every supported Python version, and uploads the artifacts to the test package index under a pre-release version.

The owner then installs the candidate into a fresh virtual directory on at least two operating systems and runs the smoke script in `scripts/smoke/`. The smoke script adds a few items, moves stock between two locations, runs a report, and exports the result. It takes under a minute. If anything differs from the expected output checked into the repository, the candidate is discarded and a new one is cut after the fix lands.

prose.heading: Release step 3: verification
prose.text:
Verification is where a second maintainer, not the release owner, signs off. They read the summary in the tracking issue, pick the three riskiest changes, and try each one by hand against the candidate. Risk here means anything that touches how quantities are stored, how the ledger is replayed, or how existing data files are read by a newer version.

The verifier also opens a data directory created by the previous release and runs the candidate against it. Upgrades must be silent: no prompts, no rewrites of the user's files unless the release explicitly ships a migration, and no change in totals. The verifier records what they checked in the tracking issue. A sign-off that only says "looks good" is sent back.

prose.heading: Release step 4: publication
prose.text:
Publication is a single manual approval in the release workflow. The workflow uses trusted publishing to the package index, so no maintainer holds a long-lived upload token, and nobody uploads artifacts by hand. After approval the workflow pushes the version tag, publishes the wheel and source distribution, and drafts the GitHub release from the summary in the tracking issue.
