The owner edits the draft for tone, links the notable pull requests, and publishes it. Then they close the tracking issue, unfreeze `main` in the maintainers channel, and open the tracking issue for the next version with an empty checklist. If publication fails halfway, do not retry blindly; ask in the channel first, because the index does not allow reusing a version number.

prose.heading: Patch releases
prose.text:
A patch release fixes a regression or a data-safety bug in the latest minor version and nothing else. It is cut from a short-lived branch named after the version, which starts at the last release tag. Fixes land on `main` first and are cherry-picked onto the branch, so the two never drift.

Patch releases follow the same four stages as a normal release, but the freeze is usually a few hours instead of a few days. The verifier focuses on the single change and on the upgrade path from the previous patch. We do not backport fixes to older minor versions. Users on an older line are asked to upgrade, and the upgrade path is something we test on every release precisely so that this request is reasonable.

prose.heading: Yanking a release
prose.text:
If a published version corrupts quantities, loses ledger entries, or cannot read data written by the previous version, we yank it from the package index within the same day. Yanking keeps the files available for pinned installs but stops new resolvers from picking the version.

The maintainer who yanks posts a pinned issue that names the affected version, describes who is affected in plain words, and says which version to use instead. A patch release with the fix follows as soon as it passes verification. We never delete a published version and never reuse its number. The post-incident note goes in `docs/incidents/` and is written blamelessly: what happened, how we noticed, what we changed so that it cannot happen the same way again.

prose.heading: CI pipeline overview
prose.text:
Every pull request runs the same pipeline, defined in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It has four jobs: lint, suite, package, and docs. Lint runs the formatter and the linter in check mode. Suite runs the full test suite on the oldest and newest supported Python versions on Linux, and on the newest version on macOS and Windows. Package builds the wheel and the source distribution and installs the wheel into an empty directory to run the smoke script. Docs builds the documentation site with warnings treated as failures.

All four jobs must be green before review approval counts. The pipeline is designed to finish in under eight minutes on a cold cache. If a change makes it slower than that, say so in the pull request and explain why; a slow pipeline is a cost that every contributor pays on every push.

prose.heading: Why the CI matrix looks the way it does
prose.text:
We do not run the full product of every Python version and every operating system. That would triple the run time and, in our history, has caught almost nothing that the reduced matrix misses. The oldest supported version catches use of newer language features; the newest catches deprecations early; the non-Linux runners catch path separators, file locking, and line ending differences in data files.

A nightly workflow runs the full matrix and opens an issue automatically when it fails. Whoever is on triage that week picks up the issue. If you touch file locking or anything platform-specific, ask a maintainer to trigger the nightly workflow on your branch before merging rather than waiting for it to find the problem after the fact.

prose.heading: Flaky jobs
prose.text:
A job that fails and then passes on retry without a code change is flaky, and flaky jobs are bugs. Do not simply re-run the pipeline until it goes green and merge. Re-run it once to confirm the flake, then open an issue with the job name, a link to the failing run, and the part of the output that differs between the runs.

Most flakes in this repository have come from three sources: tests that depend on the order of directory listings, tests that share a temporary data directory, and tests that rely on wall-clock sleeps to wait for a file lock. If your change adds any of those patterns, reviewers will ask you to remove it. A test is quarantined only by a maintainer, only with a linked issue, and only for a single release cycle.

prose.heading: CI caching
prose.text:
The pipeline caches the package download directory keyed on the lock file hash and the Python version. It does not cache build outputs or the virtual directory itself, because stale build outputs have caused confusing passes in the past.

If you change the lock file, the first run on your branch will be slower. That is expected. If a run seems to be using an outdated dependency after a lock file change, check that the cache key actually changed before assuming the cache is wrong. Never add a manual cache-busting step to the workflow; ask a maintainer to clear the cache from the repository's Actions page instead.

prose.heading: How review works
prose.text:
Every pull request needs one approving review from a maintainer, and changes to storage, the ledger, or packaging need two. Review is about whether the change is correct, whether it fits the existing design, and whether the next person can understand it. Style is the formatter's job; reviewers do not leave comments about formatting.

Reviewers aim to respond within two working days. If a pull request has waited longer, ping the reviewer once in the pull request, then once in the maintainers channel. Authors respond to every comment, either with a change or with a reply that explains why not. Resolving a thread without a reply is considered rude here. When the conversation goes past three rounds on one point, move it to a short call or a design issue rather than continuing in comments.

prose.heading: What reviewers look for
prose.text:
Reviewers in this repository follow roughly the same checklist. First, does the pull request description say what changed and why, in words a user could follow? Second, is there a test that would fail without the change? Third, does the change keep data written by older versions readable? Fourth, is the diff limited to what the description promises?

The fourth point is where most pull requests get stuck. A fix for a report rounding issue that also renames variables across the reports package is two pull requests. Split them. Reviewers are much faster on small, focused diffs, and a focused diff is far easier to revert if something goes wrong after release.

prose.heading: Review when an agent wrote the change
prose.text:
Pull requests written with an AI agent are reviewed exactly like any other pull request, with one addition: the human who opens the pull request is the author and is accountable for every line. They must have read the whole diff and be able to answer questions about it without going back to the agent.

Agents working in this repository should keep diffs small and surface uncertainty in the pull request description rather than hiding it. If the agent made an assumption about the intended behaviour, the description should name the assumption. Reviewers will ask about anything that looks generated without purpose, such as defensive branches for inputs that cannot occur or abstractions with a single caller.

prose.heading: Who owns what
prose.text:
Ownership in `stock` is recorded in `.github/CODEOWNERS` and is deliberately coarse. One maintainer owns the domain models and the ledger, one owns the storage backends, one owns the command layer and reports, and one owns packaging, CI, and releases. Documentation is shared, and any maintainer can approve docs-only changes.

Ownership means the owner is the default reviewer and the person who makes the final call when there is disagreement inside their area. It does not mean that others should stay away. Contributions across areas are welcome, and owners are expected to explain their reasoning when they decline a change. When an owner steps back, the maintainers agree on a replacement in the monthly sync and update the file in the same week.

prose.heading: Issue triage flow
prose.text:
New issues arrive with the `needs-triage` label from the issue templates. One maintainer is on triage each week, rotating in the order listed in `MAINTAINERS.md`. The triager reads every new issue within two working days and does one of four things: asks for more information, labels it as a bug with a severity, labels it as an enhancement and links any related discussion, or closes it with a short, friendly reason.

A bug needs a reproduction before it gets a severity. A good reproduction is a short sequence of `stock` commands run against an empty data directory, together with the version and platform. If the reporter cannot provide one, the triager tries to build it. Issues waiting on the reporter for more than thirty days are closed with an invitation to reopen.

prose.heading: Bug severity
prose.text:
We use three severities. Severity one means data loss, wrong totals, or a crash that prevents any command from running; it blocks the next release and usually triggers a patch release. Severity two means a feature does not work as documented but there is a workaround. Severity three is everything else, including cosmetic problems in reports and confusing wording.

Severity is about impact on users, not about how hard the fix is. A one-line fix can be severity one, and a severity three bug can take a week. When in doubt between two levels, pick the higher one; it is easy to lower later and costly to discover too late that a bug was more serious than it looked.

prose.heading: Labels
prose.text:
Labels are few on purpose. Area labels match the code ownership areas: `area/models`, `area/storage`, `area/commands`, `area/reports`, `area/packaging`, and `area/docs`. Kind labels are `bug`, `enhancement`, `question`, and `chore`. Status labels are `needs-triage`, `needs-info`, `accepted`, and `blocked`.

The `good first issue` label is only applied by a maintainer who has written down, in the issue, which files are likely to change and what a test for the change would look like. An issue without that guidance is not a good first issue, however small it seems. Please do not invent new labels in pull requests or issues; propose them in the maintainers channel first.

prose.heading: Python version support policy
prose.text:
`stock` supports every CPython version that is still receiving security updates from the core developers at the time of a release. When a version reaches end of life, we drop it in the next minor release, not in a patch release. The minimum supported version is declared in the project metadata and in the README, and both must change in the same pull request.

We add a new Python version to the CI matrix as soon as its first release candidate is available, but we only claim support for it after the final release and one green nightly run. PyPy and other implementations are not tested and not supported, although we accept small, well-contained fixes for them if they do not add maintenance cost.

prose.heading: Dependency policy
prose.text:
The runtime package depends on the Python standard library only, and that is a design goal rather than an accident. `stock` is often installed on shared machines in warehouses and small offices where adding a dependency means asking an administrator, and a dependency-free wheel removes that friction. It also keeps the attack surface small and upgrades predictable.

Development dependencies are allowed: the formatter, the linter, the documentation builder, and the coverage tool. They are pinned in the lock file and updated by the automated dependency workflow once a month. Adding a new development dependency needs a short justification in the pull request and approval from the packaging owner. Adding a runtime dependency needs a design issue and agreement from all maintainers.

prose.heading: Updating development dependencies
prose.text:
The automated dependency workflow opens one pull request per month that bumps every development dependency in the lock file. The packaging owner reviews it. If the new formatter or linter version changes how existing code looks, that reformatting goes in its own commit inside the same pull request, so the history stays readable.

Do not bump development dependencies by hand in an unrelated pull request. If you need a newer tool for your change, open a separate pull request for the bump first. This keeps the diff of your real change clean and makes it obvious, if something breaks later, whether the tool or the code is responsible.

prose.heading: Reporting a security problem
prose.text:
Please do not open a public issue for a security problem. Use the private vulnerability reporting form on the repository's Security tab, or write to the address in `SECURITY.md`. A maintainer acknowledges the report within three working days and agrees with the reporter on a timeline for a fix and a disclosure.

For `stock`, the realistic risks are reading or writing files outside the data directory, a crafted data file that makes a command consume unbounded memory, and report templates that can be made to include content from other files. Reports about any of those are very welcome. We credit reporters in the GitHub security advisory unless they ask us not to.

prose.heading: How security fixes are shipped
prose.text:
Security fixes are developed in a private fork created from the advisory, reviewed by two maintainers there, and merged to `main` only at the moment the patch release is cut. The release follows the usual four stages, but the freeze and verification happen in the private fork so the fix is not visible early.

After publication, the advisory is made public with the affected version range, the fixed version, and a plain description of the impact. We request a CVE identifier when the issue can affect data on disk or can be triggered by a file that a user received from someone else. Agents must never discuss an unpublished advisory in a public pull request, issue, or commit message.

prose.heading: Onboarding a new contributor
prose.text:
A new contributor should be able to go from a fresh clone to a green local run of the suite in about ten minutes. The steps are in `CONTRIBUTING.md`: create a virtual directory with the oldest supported Python, install the development dependencies from the lock file, and run `make check`. If any of that takes longer or fails on a clean machine, that is a bug in our onboarding and we want to hear about it.

After the setup, we suggest reading the architecture page in the docs, then the domain models, then one command from start to finish, for example `stock move`. That path touches the models, the ledger, a storage backend, and the command layer, and it is the quickest way to see how the pieces fit together before changing any of them.

prose.heading: Your first pull request
prose.text:
For a first contribution, pick an issue labelled `good first issue` and leave a comment saying you are working on it, so nobody duplicates the effort. Ask questions in the issue rather than in private messages, because the answers usually save the next person time too.

Keep the first pull request small. A maintainer will pair on the review with you, and may push small fixups directly to your branch if you allow edits from maintainers; they will always say what they changed and why. Once the pull request merges, you will be added to the contributors list in the README in the next release.

prose.heading: Working on reports
prose.text:
Reports are the part of `stock` that users see most, and the part where small changes cause the most surprise. A report reads the current state of items and the ledger through the query layer, groups and totals it, and hands the rows to a renderer. Reports never write to storage, and they never call a backend directly.

When you change a report, check three things before opening a pull request: that the totals match the ledger for the sample data set in `tests/data/sample/`, that rounding of quantities follows the unit of measure for each item, and that an empty data directory produces an empty report rather than nothing at all. The golden files for each report live next to the sample data; update them in the same pull request and mention it in the description so the reviewer looks at them.

prose.heading: The export command family
prose.text:
The export commands turn the current state into a file that another tool can read: comma-separated values for spreadsheets, a plain table for email, and a full archive that another `stock` installation can read back. All of them share one pipeline: select rows through the query layer, map them to a flat record, and write the records through a writer chosen by the export format.

New export formats are added by adding a writer, not by adding a new command. The writer gets the flat records and nothing else, which keeps it testable without storage. If a new format needs data that the flat record does not carry, extend the record and every existing writer in the same pull request, so the formats never drift apart.

prose.heading: Export compatibility
prose.text:
Exported files are read by other programs we do not control, so the column order and column names of the comma-separated export are part of the public interface. Adding a column at the end is a minor change. Renaming, removing, or reordering a column is a breaking change and needs a major version.

The archive format carries its own version number in its header. Every release must be able to read archives written by any earlier release of the same major version. The compatibility suite reads a set of archives produced by past releases, stored under `tests/data/archives/`; when you cut a release, add an archive written by the new version to that directory.

prose.heading: Performance budget
prose.text:
`stock` is meant to feel instant on the data sizes our users actually have, which is up to about fifty thousand items and a few hundred thousand ledger entries. The performance budget is that any read-only command finishes in under half a second on that size on a modest laptop, and any write command in under one second, including the time to start the interpreter.

The benchmark script in `scripts/bench/` generates a data directory of that size and times the common commands. Run it before and after any change to storage, the ledger, or the query layer, and paste both numbers into the pull request. A regression of more than ten percent needs either a fix or an explicit agreement from the storage owner.

prose.heading: Where the budget came from
prose.text:
The budget was set after a user report in the second year of the project. A small hardware shop had grown to about forty thousand items, and `stock count` took nine seconds, mostly because every command replayed the entire ledger from the first entry. The fix was the snapshot mechanism: the ledger periodically writes a checkpoint of all quantities, and replay starts from the latest checkpoint.

That episode taught us that performance problems arrive slowly and are noticed late, by users who do not file issues quickly. The benchmark and the budget exist so that we notice first. They are not a target to optimise towards; they are a floor we refuse to go below.

prose.heading: Startup cost
prose.text:
Most `stock` commands do very little work, so interpreter startup and module loading are a large share of their run time. Keep the command layer lazy: a command module should only load the storage backend and the report renderers when the command actually needs them. A new top-level dependency between packages can add tens of milliseconds to every command, which is easy to miss in review.

The benchmark reports startup time separately for this reason. If your change adds more than a few milliseconds to it, look at what your new code pulls in at module load and move it inside the function that uses it.

prose.heading: Project history
prose.text:
`stock` started as a single script that one of the original maintainers wrote for a bicycle repair shop that tracked parts in a spreadsheet. The script read the spreadsheet, applied a list of moves, and wrote it back. It grew a ledger after the spreadsheet was overwritten by mistake one Saturday and a week of counts was lost.

The first public release split the script into the package layout we still use: models, ledger, storage backends, commands, and reports. The decision to stay free of third-party runtime packages dates from that release, because the shop's machine had no internet access and every install was done from a USB stick.

prose.heading: Why there is a ledger
prose.text:
Early versions stored only current quantities. That was simple, but it made it impossible to answer the questions users kept asking: who moved this, when did we last count that shelf, and why does the number differ from last month. The ledger replaced direct edits of quantities with an append-only list of movements, and quantities became the result of replaying it.

The ledger is the source of truth. Quantities in the current-state tables are a cache derived from it. Any change that writes a quantity without writing a ledger entry is rejected in review, however convenient it seems. If the cache and the ledger ever disagree, the repair command rebuilds the cache from the ledger and never the other way round.

prose.heading: How the storage backends came to be
prose.text:
The first backend wrote plain text files, one per table, because users wanted to open them in a text editor. The second, a SQLite backend, arrived when a user with several thousand items found the text files too slow to rewrite on every change. An in-memory backend followed for tests and for the benchmark.

We kept the text backend even after SQLite became the default, because some users rely on being able to read and diff their data with ordinary tools. All backends implement the same small interface and pass the same contract suite. Adding a fourth backend is possible but has never been accepted, because each one multiplies the work of every storage change.

prose.heading: Roadmap
prose.text:
The roadmap lives in a pinned GitHub discussion and is updated after each monthly maintainers sync. It lists at most five themes for the next two minor releases. At the moment the themes are multi-location transfers in a single movement, better reports for slow-moving items, a read-only web view built on the same query layer, faster replay for very large ledgers, and clearer upgrade guides.

An item on the roadmap is a direction, not a promise. If you want to work on one of the themes, comment on the discussion first so a maintainer can point you to the design issue and tell you whether someone else has started. Work that is not on the roadmap is still welcome, but large features outside it may wait for a design discussion before review.

prose.heading: Design issues
prose.text:
Changes that affect the data format, the public library interface, the ledger, or more than one ownership area start with a design issue before any code. The design issue states the problem from a user's point of view, the proposed behaviour, what stays compatible, and what does not. It does not need to be long; one page is usually enough.

Maintainers aim to reply to a design issue within a week. Once the area owner marks it `accepted`, implementation can start. Pull requests that implement a large change without an accepted design issue are not rejected outright, but expect the review to start with the design discussion, which is slower than having it first.

prose.heading: How to approach a task in this repository
prose.text:
Before changing anything, read the part of the code the task touches and find the existing pattern for the same kind of change. Most tasks in `stock` have a precedent: a new report looks like the existing reports, a new export format looks like the existing writers, a new movement kind looks like the existing kinds. Follow the precedent unless the task says otherwise.

State a short plan before editing: which files change, which test proves the change, and how you will check it. Then make the smallest change that satisfies the task. If you discover that the task needs a decision that the issue does not cover, stop and ask in the issue rather than choosing silently. Unasked-for refactors, renames, and reformatting make the diff harder to review and are usually sent back.

prose.heading: Verifying your work
prose.text:
Run `make check` before you say a change is ready. It runs the formatter, the linter, and the full suite, the same as the lint and suite jobs in CI. For changes to storage or the ledger, also run the contract suite against every backend with `make contract` and the benchmark script described in the performance section.

If you could not run something, say so plainly in the pull request description and explain why. A description that says "tests pass" when only part of the suite was run costs reviewers far more time than an honest "I ran the models and ledger suites; I could not run the Windows-specific tests locally".

prose.heading: What done means
prose.text:
A change is done when it is merged, not when the code is written. For a pull request to be mergeable here, it must have a description that says what changed and why, a test that would fail without the change, green CI, the required approvals, and updated documentation if the behaviour a user sees has changed.

For anything that touches data on disk, done also means the upgrade path has been checked: a data directory created by the latest release still opens and reports the same totals. For a new command or report, done means it appears in the docs index and in the README's feature list. Reviewers will not approve a change that leaves any of these for a follow-up pull request unless there is a linked issue and the follow-up is trivial.

prose.heading: Working with the maintainers
prose.text:
The maintainers meet once a month in a public video call, and the notes are posted in the repository's discussions within a day. The agenda is open: anyone can add an item to the pinned agenda discussion up to two days before the call. Typical items are roadmap changes, design issues that are stuck, and proposals to change the release process.

Between calls, the maintainers channel is the place for quick coordination, and GitHub is the place for anything that needs a record. If a decision is made in a chat or a call, someone writes it down in the relevant issue the same day. Decisions that exist only in someone's memory tend to get made again, differently.

prose.heading: Becoming a maintainer
prose.text:
New maintainers are invited by the existing maintainers after a sustained period of good contributions, usually around six months. Good contributions here means more than code: careful reviews, triage, documentation, and patient answers to users all count, and some of our best maintainers started with docs.

An invitation is discussed in the monthly sync and needs agreement from every current maintainer. A new maintainer starts with review rights in one area and joins the triage rotation after a month. Maintainers who become inactive for six months are moved to emeritus status, with thanks, and can return whenever they like.

prose.heading: Community norms
prose.text:
Everyone who takes part in `stock` follows the code of conduct in `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`. In practice that means assuming good intent, being patient with people who are new to Python or to inventory work, and keeping criticism about the code rather than the person.

Many of our users are not programmers. They run small shops, workshops, and stock rooms, and they file issues in the words they have. Answer them in plain language, do not close an issue only because it lacks technical detail, and thank people for reports even when the report turns out to be a misunderstanding. A misunderstanding is often a sign that the docs need work.

prose.heading: Questions and discussions
prose.text:
Questions about how to use `stock` belong in GitHub Discussions, in the Q&A category, not in issues. Ideas that are not yet concrete enough for an issue go in the Ideas category. The triager moves misplaced issues to Discussions with a short note, and that is not a rejection.

Maintainers check Discussions at least once a week, but much of the answering is done by other users, which we value. If you answer a question and realise the docs could have answered it, open a small docs pull request and link it from the answer. Over time that has been the single most effective way to improve the documentation.

prose.heading: Commit history
prose.text:
We merge pull requests with squash merges, so the pull request title becomes the commit subject on `main`. Write the title in the imperative mood and keep it short: "Add reorder report" rather than "Added a new report for reordering". The squash commit body is the pull request description, trimmed of checklists.

Inside your branch, commit however you like. Reviewers read the diff, not the individual commits. The one case that differs is a change that mixes a mechanical step with a real change, such as moving a module and then editing it; keep those as separate commits so the reviewer can view them one at a time, and say so in the description.

prose.heading: Branches
prose.text:
Work happens on short-lived branches off `main`. Name a branch after what it does, with a kind prefix: `fix/negative-count-after-move`, `feat/reorder-report`, `docs/upgrade-guide`. Branches for patch releases are named after the version and are created only by maintainers.

Rebase your branch on `main` when it falls behind rather than merging `main` into it; that keeps the diff easy to read. Delete branches after they merge. A branch that has not moved in a month is likely to be stale, and a maintainer may ask whether it is still needed before closing the associated pull request.

prose.heading: Pull request descriptions
prose.text:
Use the pull request template. It asks for a summary, the reason for the change, how it was verified, and any compatibility notes. The summary is for a user reading the release page; the reason is for the reviewer; the verification section is for whoever has to debug this change in a year.

Link the issue the pull request closes with a closing keyword so it closes on merge. If the pull request only partly addresses an issue, say "Part of" instead, and describe what remains. Screenshots are welcome for report changes; paste the before and after output of the command as text rather than as images, so it stays searchable.

prose.heading: Draft pull requests
prose.text:
Open a pull request as a draft when you want early feedback on direction rather than a full review. Say in the description which question you want answered: for example, whether a new movement kind should be a separate model or a variant of an existing one. Reviewers look at drafts when they have time, but they do not leave line-level comments on them unless asked.

Mark the pull request ready for review only when CI is green and the description is complete. Moving a pull request back and forth between draft and ready many times makes it hard for reviewers to know when to look, so try to finish the open questions while it is still a draft.

prose.heading: Documentation workflow
prose.text:
The documentation site is built from `docs/` and published by the docs workflow on every merge to `main`. Pages are grouped into tutorials, how-to guides, reference, and background, and each new page goes into exactly one of those groups. Tutorials are for first-time users, how-to guides answer one concrete question, reference describes every command and model, and background explains why things are the way they are.

When you change user-visible behaviour, update the reference page in the same pull request. When you add a new command, also add or update a how-to guide that uses it. The docs job in CI fails on broken internal links and on pages that are not reachable from the index, so you will find out quickly if something is missing.

prose.heading: Writing style for docs
prose.text:
Write the docs in plain, short sentences, in the second person, and in the present tense. Use the words our users use: item, location, count, move, and supplier, rather than internal names from the code. Explain a concept once on its background page and link to it elsewhere, instead of repeating the explanation in several places.

Every how-to guide starts from an empty data directory or from the sample data set, so a reader can follow it exactly. Command examples show both the command and what the user sees afterwards. If the result depends on the platform, show the Linux variant and note the difference in a sentence below it.

prose.heading: Upgrade guides
prose.text:
Every minor or major release that changes something a user might notice gets an upgrade guide in `docs/upgrading/`. The guide lists what changed, what the user needs to do, and what happens if they do nothing. For most releases the honest answer to the last question is "nothing breaks", and saying so plainly is reassuring.

The release owner writes the guide during the freeze, based on the bucketed list of merged pull requests. The verifier follows the guide literally while checking the candidate. If following the guide does not work, the guide is wrong, and fixing it is part of verification.

prose.heading: The sample data set
prose.text:
`tests/data/sample/` holds a small, realistic data set: about two hundred items across three locations, with a year of movements, two suppliers, and a few deliberate oddities such as an item counted at zero and an item that was moved and moved back on the same day. It is used by the report golden files, the docs examples, and the smoke script.

Change the sample data only when a feature genuinely needs a new case, and regenerate every golden file that depends on it in the same pull request. Never add real customer data to it, even with names changed. The generator script that built it is kept next to it, and it is the preferred way to extend the set.

prose.heading: The storage contract suite
prose.text:
Every storage backend runs the same contract suite, which lives in `tests/contract/`. It describes what a backend must do in terms of the backend interface only: write a movement and read it back, list items in a stable order, survive a reopen, and refuse to write when another process holds the lock. The suite is parameterised over all backends, so a new test automatically runs everywhere.

When you change backend behaviour, change the contract first and watch it fail on every backend, then update each backend until it passes. A behaviour that only one backend has is a bug, either in that backend or in the contract. Never skip a contract test for a single backend without a linked issue and a maintainer's agreement.

prose.heading: Data migrations
prose.text:
When a release changes how data is laid out on disk, it ships a migration. Migrations live in `stock/migrations/`, are numbered in order, and run automatically the first time a newer version opens an older data directory. Each migration makes a backup copy of the files it touches before it changes anything, and it records its number in the data directory so it never runs twice.

A migration must be safe to interrupt. If the process stops halfway, the next run must either complete the migration or roll back to the backup. Migrations are reviewed by the storage owner and verified during the release with a copy of a real-sized data directory. We never ship a migration that cannot be undone by putting the backup files back.

prose.heading: Deprecating library behaviour
prose.text:
Some users call `stock` as a library from their own scripts, so the public interface of the package follows a deprecation policy. A public function, class, or argument is deprecated in one minor release, emits a deprecation warning that names the replacement, and is removed no earlier than the next major release.

The public interface is whatever is documented on the reference pages. Anything else is internal and may change in any release, even if it is reachable. If you find yourself relying on an internal name from outside the package, open an issue asking for it to become public rather than depending on it quietly.

prose.heading: Versioning
prose.text:
`stock` follows semantic versioning with the usual reading: major for breaking changes to the data format, the export formats, or the documented library interface; minor for new features; patch for fixes. The version is defined in exactly one place in the project metadata and read from there at runtime.

Pre-release versions use the standard suffixes for alphas, betas, and release candidates. Candidates from the release workflow go only to the test index, never to the main index. Do not change the version in a normal pull request; the release workflow sets it during the candidate stage.

prose.heading: What we support
prose.text:
We support the latest minor release only. Bugs reported against older versions are first checked against the latest release; if they are already fixed, the triager says so and closes the issue. If they still exist, the fix goes into the next release as usual.

We support the three platforms in the CI matrix: Linux, macOS, and Windows. Other platforms often work, and we accept small fixes for them, but we cannot promise to keep them working. We also do not support running two different versions of `stock` against the same data directory at the same time; the lock prevents most damage, but the results are not defined.

prose.heading: Incident reviews
prose.text:
When a release causes a severity one bug, the maintainers write an incident review within two weeks of the fix. The review is a short page in `docs/incidents/` with a timeline, the user impact, how the bug got past review and verification, and the changes we made to the process or the tests.

Reviews are blameless. They describe what the process allowed, not who made a mistake, because anyone following the same process could have made the same one. The most valuable section is usually the one about detection: how long it took us to find out, and whether a user had to tell us. Every review so far has added at least one case to the contract suite or the compatibility suite.

prose.heading: Decision records
prose.text:
Significant decisions are recorded in `docs/decisions/` as short numbered pages. Each one names the decision, the alternatives that were considered, and the reasons for the choice. Examples include keeping the runtime free of third-party packages, making the ledger the source of truth, and choosing squash merges.

Decision records are never edited after they are accepted, other than to mark them as superseded by a later record. If you disagree with a recorded decision, open a design issue that proposes a new record; do not argue against the old one in an unrelated pull request. Agents should read the relevant records before proposing a change that seems to contradict one.

prose.heading: Glossary of process terms
prose.text:
A few words have a specific meaning in our process. The freeze is the period during a release when only regression fixes merge. A candidate is a build published to the test index for verification. The verifier is the second maintainer who signs off on a candidate. The triager is the maintainer on the weekly triage rotation. The owner is the maintainer listed for an area in the code owners file.

In the domain, a movement is a single ledger entry that changes the quantity of one item at one location. A count is a movement that sets a quantity after a physical check. A checkpoint is the stored snapshot of all quantities that replay starts from. Using these words consistently in issues and pull requests makes discussions much quicker to follow.

prose.heading: Day-to-day local workflow
prose.text:
The `Makefile` is the entry point for everything you do locally. `make check` runs the formatter, the linter, and the suite. `make fmt` reformats the code. `make docs` builds the documentation site and serves it locally. `make bench` runs the benchmark against a generated data directory. `make contract` runs the storage contract suite against every backend.

The targets are thin wrappers over the underlying tools, so you can always run the tools directly if you prefer, but CI uses the targets. If you add a new step that CI should run, add it as a target first and then call the target from the workflow. That way local runs and CI stay in step.

prose.heading: When something takes too long
prose.text:
If a task is taking much longer than you expected, stop and write down what you have learned before going further. Post a short note in the issue: what you tried, what you found, and what you think the remaining work is. Very often a maintainer knows a shortcut, or the task turns out to be bigger than the issue suggested and should be split.

This applies to agents as much as to people. An agent that has made three attempts at the same fix without success should report back with what it observed rather than trying a fourth variation. A clear account of a failed attempt is useful to the next person; a large, uncertain diff is not.

prose.heading: Finishing and handing over
prose.text:
When you hand a change over for review, the pull request should stand on its own. A reviewer should not need to read the issue thread, a chat, or your local notes to understand what changed and how you checked it. Put the essentials in the description, and remove scratch files, debugging leftovers, and commented-out code from the diff.

If you stop working on something before it is finished, say so in the pull request or issue and describe where you left it. Unassign yourself so someone else can pick it up. A half-finished branch with a clear note is a gift to the next contributor; a silent one is a puzzle.
